subject.name: Discrete Structure
subject.description: Operations, groups, mappings, rings and fields.

resources: Proofs, relations, counting, recurrences and graphs
Open textbook: groups, rings, homomorphisms and fields

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Operations & algebraic structures
topics.brief: An algebraic structure consists of a nonempty set with one or more specified operations. An internal binary operation maps S × S to S.
topics.hinglish: Set ke saath operation define karna zaroori hai. Sirf elements likhne se structure specify nahi hota.
points: Unary operation: S → S; binary: S × S → S; n-ary: S^n → S.
Closure means the result remains in the set for every allowed input.
Subtraction is closed on integers but not on natural numbers.
A rule involving division may fail if some allowed denominator is zero.
topics.question: Is a*b = a − b a binary operation on integers? Is it one on natural numbers?
steps: For integers a,b, the difference is always an integer, so it is closed.
The expression is defined for every pair of integers; hence it is a binary operation on Z.
For natural numbers, choose a=1 and b=2. The result is −1.
Since −1 is not natural, the rule is not an internal binary operation on N.
topics.mcq: Which is closed on Z?
topics.explanation: The difference of two integers is always an integer.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Closure, associativity & commutativity
topics.brief: A property must hold for every element of the set. A single counterexample disproves it.
topics.hinglish: Commutative mein order badalta hai; associative mein brackets. Dono ko mix mat karo.
points: Commutativity: a*b = b*a.
Associativity: (a*b)*c = a*(b*c).
Expand both sides using the defined operation, not ordinary multiplication.
A Cayley table symmetric about the main diagonal indicates commutativity, but not necessarily associativity.
topics.question: On Z, let a*b = a + b + 1. Prove closure, commutativity and associativity.
steps: Closure: a+b+1 is an integer when a and b are integers.
Commutativity: a*b = a+b+1 = b+a+1 = b*a.
Left grouping: (a*b)*c = (a+b+1)+c+1 = a+b+c+2.
Right grouping: a*(b*c) = a+(b+c+1)+1 = a+b+c+2; therefore associative.
topics.mcq: A symmetric operation table directly establishes:
topics.explanation: Symmetry shows the output is unchanged when row and column inputs are swapped.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Identity, inverses & operation tables
topics.brief: An identity works on both sides. The inverse of an element combines with it to give that identity.
topics.hinglish: Identity hamesha 0 ya 1 nahi hoti; defined operation ki equation solve karo.
points: Identity e satisfies a*e = e*a = a for every a.
An inverse b satisfies a*b = b*a = e.
In a Cayley table, an identity row/column repeats the headings.
Check inverses belong to the given set.
topics.question: For a*b = a+b+1 on Z, find the identity and inverse of a.
steps: Set a*e = a+e+1 = a, giving e = −1.
Check e*a = −1+a+1 = a as well.
b is an integer and works on both sides. For a=3, the inverse is −5.
topics.mcq: For a*b=a+b+1, the identity is:
topics.explanation: Substituting −1 leaves every a unchanged.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Semigroups, monoids & submonoids
topics.brief: A semigroup has an associative binary operation. A monoid adds an identity. A submonoid is a subset that forms a monoid with the same identity.
topics.hinglish: Semigroup = closure + associativity. Identity add karo to monoid.
points: (positive integers,+) is a semigroup but has no additive identity in that set.
(nonnegative integers,+) is a monoid with identity 0.
A submonoid contains the parent identity and is closed under the operation.
Associativity is inherited from the parent structure. The syllabus spelling “sunmonoid” is treated as submonoid.
topics.question: Show that even nonnegative integers form a submonoid of (N₀,+).
steps: The parent (N₀,+) is associative and has identity 0.
The subset {0,2,4,…} contains 0.
Adding 2m and 2n gives 2(m+n), another even nonnegative integer.
Associativity is inherited; therefore the subset is a submonoid.
topics.mcq: Which additional property turns a semigroup into a monoid?
topics.explanation: A monoid is an associative structure with an identity.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Groups & Abelian groups
topics.brief: A group is closed and associative, has an identity, and gives every element an inverse. An Abelian group is also commutative.
topics.hinglish: Group prove karne ke liye saare axioms check karo; commutative hona extra condition hai.
points: Use the checklist: closure, associativity, identity, inverse.
For Abelian, also check commutativity.
(Z,+) is Abelian; (Z,×) is not a group.
(nonzero rationals,×) is Abelian; zero must be excluded.
topics.question: Prove that (Z,+) is an Abelian group.
steps: Closure: the sum of integers is an integer.
Associativity: (a+b)+c = a+(b+c).
Identity: 0; inverse of a: −a, which belongs to Z.
Commutativity: a+b=b+a. All group axioms and the Abelian condition hold.
topics.mcq: Why is (Z,×) not a group?
options: Most integers lack integer multiplicative inverses
topics.explanation: For example, 2 has inverse 1/2, which is not an integer; 0 also has no inverse.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Subgroups & normal subgroups
topics.brief: A subgroup is a subset that is itself a group under the inherited operation. A normal subgroup is invariant under conjugation.
topics.hinglish: Abelian group ka har subgroup normal hota hai; general group mein extra check chahiye.
points: One-step subgroup test: nonempty H and ab⁻¹ ∈ H for all a,b ∈ H.
For additive groups, test a−b ∈ H.
Normality: gHg⁻¹ = H for all g in G, equivalently gH = Hg.
Do not confuse a subset with a subgroup: closure alone is insufficient.
topics.question: Show that 2Z is a normal subgroup of (Z,+).
steps: 2Z contains 0 and is nonempty.
For 2m,2n in 2Z, their difference 2(m−n) is in 2Z; hence it is a subgroup.
Z under addition is Abelian.
Therefore left and right cosets agree, and 2Z is normal.
topics.mcq: Every subgroup of an Abelian group is:
topics.explanation: Commutativity makes conjugation leave each subgroup unchanged.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Cyclic groups & element order
topics.brief: A cyclic group is generated by repeated application of the operation to one element.
topics.hinglish: Ek element repeat karke poora group mil jaye to group cyclic hai.
points: Additive notation: ⟨a⟩ = {ka : k is an integer}.
The order of an element is the smallest positive n giving the identity, if one exists.
In Zₙ under addition, order(a) = n/gcd(a,n).
Every cyclic group is Abelian; not every Abelian group is cyclic.
topics.question: Find the order of 2 in (Z₆,+) and decide whether it generates Z₆.
steps: Compute repeated sums modulo 6: 2,4,0.
The first return to identity 0 occurs after 3 additions.
So order(2)=3; the generated subgroup is {0,2,4}.
It does not generate all 6 elements, so 2 is not a generator of Z₆.
topics.mcq: The order of 3 in (Z₈,+) is:

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Homomorphism, isomorphism & automorphism
topics.brief: A homomorphism preserves the operation. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism; an automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure to itself.
topics.hinglish: Sirf one-one mapping hona enough nahi; operation bhi preserve hona chahiye.
points: For groups, f(a*b)=f(a)∘f(b).
Check the source and target operations explicitly.
Isomorphism requires both injectivity and surjectivity.
Automorphism has the same structure as domain and codomain.
topics.question: Show that f: (Z,+) → (2Z,+), f(n)=2n, is an isomorphism.
steps: Preservation: f(a+b)=2a+2b=f(a)+f(b).
Injective: 2a=2b implies a=b.
Surjective onto 2Z: every even integer 2k equals f(k).
All three requirements hold, so f is an isomorphism. It is not onto Z if Z is used as the codomain.
topics.mcq: A bijective homomorphism from G to itself is:
topics.explanation: An automorphism is an isomorphism of a structure with itself.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Rings, integral domains & zero divisors
topics.brief: A ring has addition and multiplication with additive Abelian-group, multiplicative associative and distributive laws.
topics.hinglish: Ring mein multiplication ke liye inverse sab elements ko zaroori nahi; field mein nonzero elements ko chahiye.
points: (R,+) is an Abelian group; multiplication is associative and distributes over addition.
Some courses require rings to have 1; state your convention.
An integral domain is a commutative ring with 1≠0 and no nonzero zero divisors.
A nonzero zero divisor a has ab=0 for some nonzero b.
topics.recall: Nonzero a,b with ab=0 → zero divisors
topics.question: Is Z₆ an integral domain? Justify with a counterexample.
steps: Z₆ with modular addition and multiplication is a commutative ring with identity.
The classes 2 and 3 are both nonzero.
There are nonzero zero divisors, so Z₆ is not an integral domain.
topics.mcq: Which pair exhibits zero divisors in Z₆?
topics.explanation: Both are nonzero, but their product is 0 modulo 6.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Fields & division rings
topics.brief: A division ring gives each nonzero element a multiplicative inverse. A field is a commutative division ring.
topics.hinglish: Field = nonzero elements ka inverse + commutative multiplication. Zero ka inverse kabhi required nahi.
points: A field has 1≠0 and commutative multiplication.
Every field is an integral domain; the converse need not hold.
Z is an integral domain but not a field because 2 has no integer inverse.
Zₚ is a field when p is prime; a division ring need not have commutative multiplication.
topics.question: Why is Z₅ a field while Z is not?
steps: Modulo 5, nonzero inverses exist: 1↔1, 2↔3 and 4↔4.
Multiplication in Z₅ is commutative, and 1≠0.
Therefore Z₅ is a field.
In Z, the nonzero element 2 would need inverse 1/2, which is not an integer; Z is not a field.
topics.mcq: Which statement is always true?
options: Every field is an integral domain
Every integral domain is a field
topics.explanation: A field has no nonzero zero divisors; integers show the converse fails.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Sets, power sets, multisets & induction
topics.brief: Sets record membership without multiplicity; multisets record counts. Induction proves a property for all integers from a starting point.
topics.hinglish: Induction: base case aur n→n+1 dono prove karo.
points: Set algebra includes union, intersection, difference and complement, with dual identities.
A finite n-element set has 2^n subsets; Cartesian products contain ordered pairs.
Distinguish finite/infinite sets, indexed classes and multisets.
Induction needs a base case and an implication P(k)⇒P(k+1).
topics.question: Prove 1+2+…+n=n(n+1)/2 for n≥1.
steps: Assume the sum to k equals k(k+1)/2.
This is the required formula for k+1; induction proves the result.
topics.mcq: A set with 4 distinct elements has how many subsets?
topics.explanation: Each of four elements has include/exclude choices.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Relations, equivalence & functions
topics.brief: Relations connect elements; functions assign exactly one output to each domain element.
topics.hinglish: One-one = injective; onto = surjective; dono = bijective.
points: Represent binary relations as pairs, matrices or directed graphs.
Equivalence relations are reflexive, symmetric and transitive and determine partitions.
Injective means distinct inputs have distinct outputs; surjective means every codomain value is reached.
Function composition applies the inner function first; an inverse function exists for a bijection. Cardinality counts set size, including infinite-set comparisons.
topics.question: Show congruence modulo 3 is an equivalence relation on Z.
steps: Reflexive: a−a=0 is divisible by 3.
Symmetric: if 3 divides a−b, it divides b−a.
Transitive: add a−b and b−c to get a−c.
Classes are residues 0,1,2 modulo 3, partitioning the integers.
topics.mcq: A function with a two-sided inverse is:
topics.explanation: Both uniqueness and coverage are needed for an inverse function.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Propositions, truth tables & proofs
topics.brief: Propositional logic combines truth-valued statements and tests whether arguments preserve truth.
topics.hinglish: Tautology har row mein true; contradiction har row mein false.
points: AND, OR and NOT build compound statements; implication p→q is equivalent to ¬p∨q.
A tautology is always true; a contradiction always false; a contingency depends on values.
To test equivalence, compare all truth-table rows.
A valid argument has no row with true premises and a false conclusion.
topics.question: Show that p∨¬p is a tautology.
steps: When p=true, ¬p=false and the OR is true.
When p=false, ¬p=true and the OR is true.
These are all possible values of p.
The expression is true in every row, hence a tautology.
topics.mcq: An implication p→q is false when:
topics.explanation: A true premise with a false conclusion is the single false implication case.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Posets, Hasse diagrams & lattices
topics.brief: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. A lattice gives every pair a greatest lower bound and least upper bound.
topics.hinglish: Antisymmetric ka matlab symmetric ka simple opposite nahi; a≤b aur b≤a se a=b.
points: A Hasse diagram omits loops and transitively implied edges; larger elements are drawn above smaller ones.
Meet is greatest lower bound; join is least upper bound.
Lattice laws include idempotence, commutativity, associativity and absorption.
A sublattice is closed under meet/join; know bounded, complemented, distributive and Boolean lattices.
topics.question: In the divisibility lattice of divisors of 12, find meet and join of 4 and 6.
steps: Divisors are {1,2,3,4,6,12}, ordered by divisibility.
Common divisors of 4 and 6 are 1 and 2; greatest is 2, the meet.
Common multiples within the set include 12, the least upper bound.
topics.mcq: In divisibility lattices, meet usually corresponds to:
topics.explanation: The greatest common divisor is the greatest common lower bound.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Counting, pigeonhole & binomial identities
topics.brief: The addition rule counts disjoint choices; the multiplication rule counts successive choices.
topics.hinglish: Ya wale disjoint options add; stages wale options multiply.
points: Permutations arrange; combinations choose without order: nCr=n!/(r!(n−r)!).
Pigeonhole: placing more than n objects in n boxes puts at least two together.
Generalized version guarantees a box with at least ceil(N/k) of N objects in k boxes.
Pascal identity: nCr=(n−1)C(r−1)+(n−1)Cr; prove by splitting subsets on a fixed element.
topics.question: Prove Pascal’s identity using subsets.
steps: Count r-element subsets of an n-element set.
Fix one distinguished element x.
Subsets containing x choose r−1 from the remaining n−1; subsets omitting x choose r from n−1.
The cases are disjoint and exhaustive, so their counts add to nCr.
topics.mcq: Choosing 3 students from 8 without roles uses:
topics.explanation: Order of selection does not matter.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Inclusion–exclusion
topics.brief: Add individual counts and subtract overlaps so each object is counted once.
topics.hinglish: A∪B count karte waqt common elements double count hote hain, isliye subtract karo.
points: For two sets: |A∪B|=|A|+|B|−|A∩B|.
For three sets add singles, subtract pair intersections, then add the triple intersection.
For divisibility, intersections use the least common multiple.
State interval endpoints and whether zero is included.
topics.question: How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 3 or 5?
steps: Multiples of 3: floor(100/3)=33.
Multiples of 5: 20.
Multiples of lcm(3,5)=15: 6.
topics.mcq: Why subtract the intersection?
topics.explanation: Adding both set sizes includes overlap twice.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Recurrences & generating functions
topics.brief: A recurrence defines a term using previous terms; initial conditions select one solution.
topics.hinglish: Characteristic roots se homogeneous solution; forcing term se particular solution.
points: For a linear constant-coefficient recurrence, substitute a_n=r^n to obtain the characteristic polynomial.
Distinct roots give sums C_i r_i^n; repeated roots require polynomial factors in n.
A total nonhomogeneous solution is homogeneous plus a particular solution.
Generating functions A(x)=Σa_nx^n convert shifted recurrences into algebraic equations; account for initial terms.
topics.question: Solve a_(n+2)−3a_(n+1)+2a_n=0, a_0=2,a_1=3.
steps: Characteristic polynomial r²−3r+2=(r−1)(r−2).
General solution a_n=C+D·2^n.
Initial conditions give C+D=2 and C+2D=3, so D=1,C=1.
Therefore a_n=1+2^n; check a_0=2 and a_1=3.
topics.mcq: A double characteristic root r contributes terms of form:
topics.explanation: Repeated roots require linearly independent polynomial factors.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Graphs, matrices & graph mappings
topics.brief: Graphs model relationships. A graph isomorphism preserves adjacency bijectively; a graph homomorphism preserves edges but need not be bijective.
topics.hinglish: Graph homomorphism aur algebraic homomorphism ka context alag rakho.
points: Know directed/undirected, weighted, simple and multigraphs, subgraphs, connectivity and complete graphs.
Adjacency matrices index vertices by vertices; incidence matrices index vertices by edges.
A graph automorphism is an isomorphism from a graph to itself.
Vertex degrees, edge count and cycle structure can disprove isomorphism, though matching these alone is not a proof.
topics.question: How many edges does a simple undirected complete graph K₅ have?
steps: Every pair of distinct vertices has exactly one edge.
Choose an unordered pair: 5C2.
Each vertex has degree 4; degree sum 20=2×10 confirms the result.
topics.mcq: A 6-vertex, 8-edge incidence matrix has dimensions:
topics.explanation: Rows represent vertices and columns represent edges.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Walks, Euler & Hamilton paths
topics.brief: Walks follow adjacent vertices. Euler routes use every edge once; Hamilton routes visit every vertex once.
topics.hinglish: Euler edges ko cover karta hai, Hamilton vertices ko.
points: A trail repeats no edge; a simple path repeats no vertex; a circuit is closed (state the convention).
A connected undirected graph has an Euler circuit if every non-isolated vertex has even degree.
Exactly two odd-degree vertices permit an Euler trail with those endpoints.
Hamilton existence has no equivalent simple even-degree test; construct or disprove a route.
topics.question: Does the path graph A–B–C have an Euler trail and a Hamilton path?
steps: Degrees are 1,2,1, giving exactly two odd vertices.
A–B–C traverses both edges once, so it is an Euler trail.
The same route visits every vertex once, so it is also a Hamilton path.
It has neither an Euler circuit nor a Hamilton cycle.
topics.mcq: For an Euler circuit in a connected undirected graph, degrees must be:
topics.explanation: Entering and leaving each vertex pairs incident edges.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Planarity, cut points & shortest paths
topics.brief: Planar graphs can be drawn without edge crossings. Cut vertices and bridges describe fragile connectivity.
topics.hinglish: Bridge edge remove karne se components badhte hain; cut vertex vertex removal se.
points: Connected planar graphs satisfy V−E+F=2, counting the outer face.
A simple planar graph with V≥3 obeys E≤3V−6; the inequality alone does not prove planarity.
A bridge increases components when removed; a cut vertex does so when removed with incident edges.
Dijkstra finds shortest paths with nonnegative edge weights; it is not a minimum spanning-tree algorithm.
topics.question: A connected planar graph has 6 vertices and 9 edges. Find faces.
steps: Write Euler’s formula 6−9+F=2.
Rearrange: F=2−6+9.
F=5, including the unbounded outer face.
This calculation assumes the given embedding is connected and planar.
topics.mcq: Dijkstra’s usual correctness requires:
topics.explanation: A negative edge can invalidate the greedy settled-distance assumption.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
topics.title: Trees, spanning trees & cut-sets
topics.brief: A tree is connected and acyclic. A spanning tree includes every vertex of a connected graph.
topics.hinglish: Spanning tree sab vertices include karta hai aur cycle nahi rakhta.
points: Any n-vertex tree has n−1 edges and a unique simple path between each pair.
Adding an edge to a tree creates a cycle; removing one separates it into two components.
Rooted trees define parent, child, depth and height; binary trees have at most two children per node.
Traversal orders are preorder, inorder and postorder. A cut-set is a set of edges whose removal disconnects the graph.
topics.recall: Spanning tree on n vertices has n−1 edges
topics.question: How many edges must be removed from a connected 7-vertex, 10-edge graph to obtain a spanning tree?
steps: A spanning tree on 7 vertices contains 6 edges.
The original graph contains 10 edges.
Remove 10−6=4 suitably chosen cycle edges.
Do not remove arbitrary bridges; the remaining graph must stay connected.
topics.mcq: Adding one non-tree edge to a tree creates:
topics.explanation: The tree already has exactly one path between the new edge’s endpoints.

units.text: Set Theory: Introduction to set theory, set operations, Algebra of Sets, Combination of sets, Duality, Finite and infinite sets, Classes of sets, Power sets, Multi sets, Cartesian Product, Representation of relations, Types of relation, Binary relation, Equivalence relations and partitions, Mathematics Induction. Function and its types: Composition of function and relations, Cardinality and inverse relations, Functions, logic and proofs injective, surjective and bijective functions.
units.title: Unit 1

units.text: Propositional Calculus: Basic operations; AND(^), OR(v), NOT(~), True value of a compound statement, propositions, tautologies, and contradictions. Partial ordering relations and lattices. Lattice theory: Partial ordering, posets, lattices as posets, properties of lattices as algebraic systems, sublattices, and some special lattices.
units.title: Unit 2

units.text: Combinations: The Basic of Counting, Pigeonhole Principles, Permutations and Combinations, Principle of Inclusion and Exclusion. Recursion and Recurrence Relation: linear recurrence relation with constant coefficients, Homogeneous solutions, Particular solutions, and Total solution of a recurrence relation using generating functions.
units.title: Unit 3

units.text: Algebraic Structures: Definition, elementary properties of Algebraic structures, examples of a Monoid, sunmonoid, semigroup, groups and rings, Homomorphism, Isomorphism and automorphism, Subgroups and Normal subgroups, Cyclic groups, Integral domain and fields, Rings, Division Ring.
units.title: Unit 4

units.text: Graphs and Trees: Introduction to graphs, Directed and undirected graphs, Homomorphic and Isomorphic graphs, Subgraphs, cut points and bridges, Multigraph and Weighted graphs, Paths and circuits, Shortest path in a weighted graph, Eulerian path and circuits, Hamilton paths and circuits, Planar graphs, Euler’s formula, Trees, Rooted trees, Spanning trees and cut-sets, Binary trees and its traversals.
units.title: Unit 5

subject.name: Data Structures & Algorithms
subject.description: Trace algorithms, draw structures and compare time complexity.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Tree basics, binary & threaded trees
topics.brief: A tree is a connected acyclic structure. A binary tree allows at most two children per node; threads can replace null links with traversal connections.
topics.hinglish: Binary tree ka matlab maximum two children; har node ke exactly two children zaroori nahi.
points: Root has no parent; leaves have no children; siblings share a parent.
A tree with n nodes has n−1 edges.
With height counted in edges, the root has depth 0 and a binary tree has at most 2^(h+1)−1 nodes.
Threaded trees can use otherwise null pointers for inorder predecessor/successor links; flags distinguish links from threads.
topics.question: A binary tree has height 3 measured in edges. Find its maximum nodes and explain a thread.
steps: Levels run from depth 0 through depth 3.
Maximum nodes per level are 1,2,4,8.
A thread uses an otherwise null link for a traversal predecessor or successor, reducing traversal-stack needs.
topics.mcq: A tree with 12 nodes has:
topics.explanation: Any finite tree with n nodes has n−1 edges.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Tree traversals & binary search trees
topics.brief: A BST keeps smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right subtree, using a defined rule for duplicates.
topics.hinglish: Inorder traversal of BST sorted order deta hai. Root placement yaad rakho: pre, in, post.
points: Preorder: root-left-right; inorder: left-root-right; postorder: left-right-root.
Searching, insertion and deletion cost O(h), where h is the tree height.
A skewed BST can have height O(n).
For a node with two children, deletion can replace the key using its inorder successor or predecessor.
topics.recall: Pre: NLR · In: LNR · Post: LRN
topics.question: Insert 40,20,60,10,30 into a BST. Give all three depth-first traversals.
steps: 40 is root; 20 is left; 60 is right; 10 and 30 are left and right children of 20.
Preorder visits root first: 40,20,10,30,60.
Inorder visits root between subtrees: 10,20,30,40,60.
Postorder visits root last: 10,30,20,60,40.
topics.mcq: Which BST traversal gives sorted keys?
topics.explanation: Left subtree keys precede the node and its larger right subtree keys.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: AVL trees & rotations
topics.brief: An AVL tree is a BST whose left and right subtree heights differ by at most one at every node.
topics.hinglish: Balance factor −1,0,+1 allowed. Imbalance type se rotation select karo.
points: Balance factor = height(left) − height(right), using one consistent convention.
LL imbalance: right rotation; RR: left rotation.
LR: left rotation on the left child, then right rotation; RL is the reverse.
Maintaining balance keeps search, insertion and deletion O(log n).
topics.question: Insert 30,20,10 into an AVL tree and fix the imbalance.
steps: Insert as a BST: 30 root, 20 left child, 10 left child of 20.
At 30, the balance factor becomes +2 under left-minus-right convention.
This is an LL imbalance; perform a right rotation at 30.
The new root is 20, with left child 10 and right child 30.
topics.mcq: The fix for an LL imbalance is:
topics.explanation: Right rotation promotes the left child and restores balance.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: B-trees & B+ trees
topics.brief: Balanced multiway search trees store many keys per node, reducing disk-access depth.
topics.hinglish: B+ tree ke leaves linked hote hain, isliye range queries efficient hoti hain.
points: B-tree keys and records can occur in internal and leaf nodes.
In a typical B+ tree, internal nodes guide search; records are stored in leaves.
B+ leaf nodes are linked for sequential and range access.
All leaves stay at the same depth. State the order/minimum-degree convention used in numerical questions.
topics.recall: B+ leaves store records and support range scans
topics.question: Why is a B+ tree useful for a database range query?
steps: Internal separator keys guide the search to the first relevant leaf.
Records reside in leaf nodes.
Linked leaves allow scanning the remaining range without restarting from the root.
High branching factor reduces height and disk-page accesses.
topics.mcq: In a typical B+ tree, complete records are stored in:
topics.explanation: Internal nodes guide the search and leaves store record entries.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Graphs & representations
topics.brief: A graph contains vertices and edges. Choose an adjacency list or matrix based on density and operations.
topics.hinglish: Matrix mein edge check fast, list mein sparse graph ki memory kam lagti hai.
points: Directed edges have orientation; undirected edges connect both ways.
Adjacency matrix takes O(V²) storage and gives O(1) edge checks.
Adjacency lists take O(V+E) storage and efficiently enumerate neighbors.
For an undirected graph, each ordinary edge contributes 2 to the total degree.
topics.question: An undirected graph has degrees 2,3,1,2. Find its edge count and choose a representation if it is sparse.
steps: Sum the degrees: 2+3+1+2=8.
By the handshaking lemma, 2E=8, so E=4.
A sparse graph has relatively few edges compared with V².
Use adjacency lists for space proportional to vertices plus edges.
topics.mcq: Adjacency-list space is:
topics.explanation: Lists store each vertex and its incident/outgoing edges.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: BFS & DFS traversal
topics.brief: BFS explores by distance layers using a queue. DFS explores deeply using recursion or a stack.
topics.hinglish: BFS queue; DFS stack. Visited mark nahi karoge to cycle mein phas sakte ho.
points: Mark discovered vertices to avoid repeated processing.
With adjacency lists, BFS and DFS take O(V+E).
BFS finds minimum edge-count paths in an unweighted graph.
Traversal order depends on neighbor ordering; state it. Restart from unvisited vertices for disconnected graphs.
topics.question: Edges are A–B, A–C, B–D, C–E. Traverse from A, taking neighbors alphabetically.
steps: BFS: visit A, enqueue B,C; visit B and enqueue D; visit C and enqueue E.
BFS order is A,B,C,D,E.
DFS: from A go to B, then D; backtrack to A, then C and E.
DFS order is A,B,D,C,E. Different neighbor orders can change valid traversal sequences.
topics.mcq: For shortest paths by edge count in an unweighted graph, use:
topics.explanation: BFS discovers vertices in increasing number of edges from the source.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Selection & bubble sort
topics.brief: Selection sort repeatedly chooses the smallest remaining value. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighboring values in the wrong order.
topics.hinglish: Selection mein minimum select karo; bubble mein adjacent compare-swap. Har pass ka result likho.
points: Selection sort makes Θ(n²) comparisons even for sorted input.
Standard selection sort is in-place and usually not stable.
Bubble sort is stable if equal elements are not swapped.
With an early-exit flag, bubble sort is O(n) best case; its average and worst cases are O(n²).
topics.recall: Selection: choose min; bubble: swap neighbors
topics.question: Perform selection sort on [5,2,4,1], showing the end of each pass.
steps: Pass 1: minimum is 1; swap with 5 → [1,2,4,5].
Pass 2: remaining minimum is 2; array unchanged.
Pass 3: remaining minimum is 4; array unchanged.
Sorted result is [1,2,4,5]. Comparisons still total 3+2+1=6.
topics.mcq: Standard selection sort on already sorted input takes:
topics.explanation: It still scans the remaining suffix for the minimum each pass.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Insertion sort
topics.brief: Insertion sort builds a sorted prefix by shifting larger values and inserting the next key.
topics.hinglish: Cards arrange karne jaisa: next key ko sorted part mein sahi jagah lagao.
points: Elements greater than the key shift one position right.
Best case O(n); average/worst O(n²).
It is in-place and stable when shifting only strictly larger keys.
Useful for small or nearly sorted inputs.
topics.recall: Sorted prefix grows one key at a time
topics.question: Trace insertion sort on [5,2,4,1].
steps: Insert 2 into [5]: shift 5 → [2,5,4,1].
Insert 4 into [2,5]: shift 5 → [2,4,5,1].
Worst-case shifts are quadratic; already sorted input needs only linear comparisons.
topics.mcq: Insertion sort is especially useful for:
topics.explanation: Few out-of-order values require few shifts.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Quick sort & partitioning
topics.brief: Quick sort partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts the smaller regions.
topics.hinglish: Pivot ke left smaller, right larger values. Partition convention clear rakho.
points: Average/expected complexity is O(n log n); worst case is O(n²).
A poor repeated pivot split causes the worst case.
Randomized pivots reduce the likelihood of consistently poor splits.
Typical array quicksort is not stable; recursion uses additional stack space.
topics.question: Partition [4,2,5,1,3] using last element 3 as pivot with Lomuto partition.
steps: Start with pivot 3 and a boundary before the first element. 4 is greater, so leave it.
2 is ≤3: move it to the left → [2,4,5,1,3].
5 is greater; 1 is ≤3: swap into the left partition → [2,1,5,4,3].
Swap pivot into the boundary position → [2,1,3,4,5]. Recursively sort [2,1] and [4,5].
topics.mcq: Quicksort worst-case time is:
topics.explanation: Repeated 0 versus n−1 splits produce quadratic work.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Merge sort & heap sort
topics.brief: Merge sort divides and merges sorted halves. Heap sort repeatedly removes the maximum from a max heap.
topics.hinglish: Merge combine karta hai; heap largest ko end mein fix karta hai. Complexity ke saath space bhi likho.
points: Merge sort has O(n log n) worst-case time; standard array implementations need O(n) auxiliary memory.
It is stable when ties take the element from the left half first.
Heap sort has O(n log n) worst-case time and can operate with O(1) auxiliary array space.
Standard heap sort is not stable. Bottom-up heap construction is O(n).
topics.recall: Merge: stable + extra memory; heap: in-place + not stable
topics.question: Merge the sorted lists [2,5] and [1,4], then compare merge sort with heap sort.
steps: Compare 2 and 1: output 1. Compare 2 and 4: output 2.
Compare 5 and 4: output 4; append remaining 5. Result [1,2,4,5].
Merge sort repeatedly performs this merge after splitting; time O(n log n), typical extra space O(n).
Heap sort builds a max heap, moves the maximum to the end repeatedly; O(n log n) time and O(1) array workspace.
topics.mcq: Which sort is typically stable?
topics.explanation: Choosing the left copy first on equal keys preserves relative order.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Hashing & collision resolution
topics.brief: Hashing maps keys to table indices. A collision occurs when different keys map to the same index.
topics.hinglish: Same slot milna normal collision hai. Chaining ya probing se resolve karo.
points: Separate chaining stores a collection of entries at each bucket.
Open addressing stores entries in the table and probes alternative slots.
Linear probing: (h(k)+i) mod m; clustering can degrade performance.
Expected O(1) access requires reasonable load and hashing assumptions; worst case can be O(n).
Load factor α = n/m. Quadratic probing and double hashing are other collision strategies.
topics.question: Insert 10,17,24 into a table of size 7 using h(k)=k mod 7 and linear probing.
steps: 10 mod 7 = 3; place 10 at index 3.
17 mod 7 = 3; index 3 is occupied, so place 17 at 4.
24 mod 7 = 3; indices 3 and 4 are occupied, so place 24 at 5.
Load factor is 3/7. Final occupied slots: 3→10, 4→17, 5→24.
topics.mcq: Linear probing is especially associated with:
topics.explanation: Contiguous runs of occupied slots tend to grow.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Data organization & algorithm analysis
topics.brief: A data structure organizes values and supports operations; complexity measures how work grows with input size.
topics.hinglish: Big-O upper bound hai, exact running seconds nahi.
points: Know traversal, insertion, deletion and update and their costs for the chosen representation.
O is an asymptotic upper bound, Ω a lower bound, Θ a tight bound.
Distinguish best, average and worst cases and state the input assumptions.
A time-space trade-off uses extra storage to reduce work or vice versa.
topics.question: Find the complexity of a loop whose ith iteration performs i operations, i=1..n.
steps: Total work is Σi = n(n+1)/2.
Expand as (n²+n)/2.
The quadratic term dominates as n grows.
Therefore the tight bound is Θ(n²).
topics.mcq: A tight asymptotic bound is written:
topics.explanation: Theta bounds the growth rate above and below by constant multiples.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Linear & binary search
topics.brief: Linear search checks values in order. Binary search halves a sorted search range.
topics.hinglish: Binary search ke liye sorted data aur efficient indexed access important hai.
points: Linear search works on unsorted sequences and has O(n) worst-case time.
Binary search compares a middle element and discards half the range; O(log n) comparisons.
Use mid=low+(high−low)/2 to avoid addition overflow in fixed-width integer code.
Update bounds so the interval shrinks; define behavior for duplicate keys.
topics.question: Find 17 in [3,8,12,17,24] using binary search.
steps: low=0,high=4; mid=2 gives 12.
17>12, so set low=3.
mid=3 gives 17; return index 3.
Two comparisons found the value; absent values eventually make low>high.
topics.mcq: Binary search on an unsorted array is:
topics.explanation: Its discard-half reasoning relies on sorted values.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Stacks, expression conversion & evaluation
topics.brief: A stack is LIFO: the most recently inserted item is removed first.
topics.hinglish: Postfix evaluate karte waqt right operand pehle pop hota hai.
points: push/pop/top are O(1) for suitable array or linked implementations.
Applications include function calls, backtracking and expression parsing.
Infix-to-postfix uses an operator stack, precedence and associativity rules.
For postfix evaluation, push operands; for an operator pop right then left, compute and push the result.
topics.question: Evaluate postfix expression 5 2 3 * +.
steps: Push 5,2,3.
Read *: pop right=3,left=2; push 6. Stack becomes [5,6].
Read +: pop 6 and 5; push 11.
The single remaining value is 11.
topics.mcq: A stack follows:
topics.explanation: Last in, first out.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Queues, circular queues & priority queues
topics.brief: A queue is FIFO. Circular indexing reuses array slots; priority queues select by priority rather than arrival alone.
topics.hinglish: Circular queue mein rear wrap hota hai; full aur empty condition clear define karo.
points: enqueue/dequeue on a circular array or linked queue can be O(1).
With one unused slot, empty is front=rear and full is (rear+1)%capacity=front.
Other representations use a count and can use all slots; do not mix conventions.
A binary-heap priority queue supports O(log n) insertion/removal and O(1) peek.
topics.question: In a circular array queue of size 5 with one reserved slot, front=2,rear=1. Is it full?
steps: Apply full condition (rear+1)%5=front.
This equals front, so the queue is full under the reserved-slot convention.
Maximum stored entries are 4, not 5.
topics.mcq: An ordinary queue follows:
topics.explanation: The first inserted element is removed first.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Singly linked lists & linked stacks/queues
topics.brief: A linked list stores nodes with data and links, so neighbors need not occupy adjacent memory.
topics.hinglish: Insertion O(1) tab hai jab correct predecessor/node pointer already available ho.
points: Traversal/search generally cost O(n); head insertion is O(1).
To delete a non-head node in a singly linked list, update its predecessor’s next link.
Linked stacks use the head; linked queues need front/rear pointers for O(1) operations.
Header/sentinel nodes simplify boundary cases; release removed nodes and update tail when needed.
topics.recall: Save next before deleting a node
topics.question: Insert 15 after node 10 in 10→20→30.
steps: Allocate a node new with data 15.
Set new.next to the old 10.next, which points to 20.
Set 10.next to new.
Result: 10→15→20→30. Reversing these updates carelessly can lose the remaining list.
topics.mcq: A known-node insertion after a singly linked node costs:
topics.explanation: Only a constant number of links changes once the location is known.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Doubly & circular linked lists
topics.brief: Doubly linked nodes have prev/next links. Circular lists connect the final node back to the start.
topics.hinglish: Circular traversal null par stop nahi hota; starting node par wapas aane par stop karo.
points: A doubly linked list supports backward traversal and deletion of a known node using its neighbors.
More links mean extra storage and more updates per insertion/deletion.
Circular lists support round-robin processing; handle the single-node case separately.
State whether a sentinel is used and update both forward and backward links when applicable.
topics.question: Delete a middle node x from a doubly linked list.
steps: Let p=x.prev and n=x.next.
Set p.next=n if p exists; otherwise update the head.
Set n.prev=p if n exists; otherwise update the tail.
Release x and never dereference it afterward.
topics.mcq: A doubly linked node normally contains:
topics.explanation: The backward link enables traversal in both directions.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: Dijkstra, Prim & spanning trees
topics.brief: Shortest-path and minimum-spanning-tree problems optimize different quantities.
topics.hinglish: Dijkstra source se distance; Prim poore spanning tree ka total weight minimize karta hai.
points: Dijkstra repeatedly settles the nearest tentative vertex, then relaxes outgoing edges; weights must be nonnegative.
Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from the current tree to an unvisited vertex.
For connected undirected weighted graphs, an MST spans all vertices with minimum total edge weight.
Heap + adjacency-list implementations run in O((V+E) log V); array/matrix forms are often O(V²).
topics.question: For undirected edges AB=1, AC=4, BC=2, find an MST and distances from A.
steps: Prim from A selects AB=1.
The cheapest crossing edge is BC=2, so MST weight=3.
Dijkstra gives distance(A)=0, distance(B)=1.
A→B→C costs 3, improving direct AC=4; distance(C)=3.
topics.mcq: Prim’s algorithm minimizes:
options: Distance from one source to each vertex
topics.explanation: Prim constructs a minimum spanning tree.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
topics.title: B-tree insertion & reconstruction
topics.brief: B-tree insertion maintains ordered keys and balanced leaves by splitting overflowing nodes. Traversals can reconstruct a unique binary tree when keys are distinct.
topics.hinglish: Order convention pehle likho; max children m ho to max keys m−1.
points: For order m defined as max children, a node stores at most m−1 keys.
Insert into the appropriate leaf; on overflow split and promote a middle key, possibly propagating to a new root.
B+ insertion promotes separator copies while records remain at leaves; deletion may borrow or merge.
Preorder’s first item is the root. Split inorder around it and recursively partition preorder; duplicates require an additional rule.
topics.question: Reconstruct a tree from preorder A B D E C and inorder D B E A C.
steps: Root is A, the first preorder item.
Inorder left of A is D B E; right is C.
Left preorder is B D E; root B has children D and E.
Right subtree is C. Check inorder D B E A C and preorder A B D E C.
topics.mcq: In preorder traversal, the first value is:
topics.explanation: Preorder visits root before either subtree.

subject.name: Universal Human Values
subject.description: Clear definitions, relationships and practical engineering examples.

resources: Course material on harmony, self-exploration and professional ethics

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Four orders of nature
topics.brief: UHV groups nature into physical/material, bio/pranic, animal and human orders to study their relationships.
topics.hinglish: Sirf four names nahi; har order ka example aur doosron se relation likho.
points: Physical/material: soil, water, air and metals.
Bio/pranic: plants and trees.
Animal: animals and birds; human: people.
Use an everyday example to show dependence and responsible participation.
topics.question: Explain the four orders of nature using a campus garden example.
steps: Identify physical resources: soil, sunlight and water.
Identify plants: grass, flowers and trees.
Identify animal life: insects and birds; identify people maintaining the garden.
Explain connections: soil supports plants, plants provide food/habitat, and people can protect or damage this cycle.
topics.mcq: A mango tree belongs to which order?
topics.explanation: Plants are classified under the bio or pranic order.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Mutual fulfilment & natural cycles
topics.brief: Harmony in nature is studied through interdependence, self-regulation and cyclical processes.
topics.hinglish: Nature ke relations ko example se samjhao: ek ka output doosre ke kaam aa sakta hai.
points: Describe how different orders support each other.
Explain a cycle such as nutrient cycling instead of giving only a slogan.
Human production should account for resource renewal, waste and other living beings.
Connect responsible use to a practical action at home, college or industry.
topics.question: Explain mutual fulfilment with a composting example.
steps: Leaves and food scraps are collected instead of being mixed with harmful waste.
Decomposition returns nutrients to soil.
The soil supports new plants, which supply food and habitat.
Human participation improves the cycle by sorting waste and avoiding pollutants; assess actual effects rather than only intentions.
topics.mcq: Which action best supports a nutrient cycle?
topics.explanation: Suitable compost returns organic matter and nutrients to the soil.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Existence as co-existence
topics.brief: In the UHV framework, existence is understood as units co-existing in all-pervading space.
topics.hinglish: Units alag pehchaan rakhti hain, par isolated nahi; relations ko samajhna main point hai.
points: Distinguish finite units from all-pervading space in the course framework.
Study relationships and participation rather than treating each unit in isolation.
Connect harmony across individual, family, society and nature/existence.
Label this as the UHV conceptual account; avoid turning it into an unsupported physics proof.
topics.question: Explain co-existence and relate it to harmony at different levels.
steps: Define co-existence in the UHV framework as units existing together in space.
Explain that units participate in relationships.
At the personal/family level, use responsible conduct and trust as examples.
At society/nature level, show how fair cooperation and responsible resource use support the larger system.
topics.mcq: Which phrase matches the UHV account of existence?
topics.explanation: Co-existence is the organizing idea of this syllabus topic.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Natural acceptance & self-exploration
topics.brief: Natural acceptance is used in UHV to examine proposals for right understanding through self-exploration and validation in living.
topics.hinglish: Pressure ya habit ko natural acceptance mat samjho. Proposal ko khud examine karo aur behavior mein verify karo.
points: Ask whether a proposed action supports mutual happiness and harmony.
Distinguish inner acceptance from immediate preference or social pressure.
Validate understanding through lived behavior and its effects.
Write a specific dilemma and explain the reasoning, not only “do good.”
topics.question: A student is pressured to copy an assignment. Apply self-exploration.
steps: Identify the conflict: short-term approval versus honest learning and fair evaluation.
Examine whether deception supports trust and mutual respect.
Choose an honest alternative: attempt the work and request help for unclear parts.
Validate the choice through improved understanding and reliable relationships rather than marks alone.
topics.mcq: Natural acceptance is best distinguished from:
options: A passing preference or peer pressure
topics.explanation: The course distinguishes natural acceptance from conditioned likes and external pressure.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Definitiveness of ethical human conduct
topics.brief: Ethical conduct combines clear values, sound policy and consistent character in real situations.
topics.hinglish: Values kya important hai batati hain; policy decision guide karti hai; character action mein dikhta hai.
points: Values express the purpose of participation and relationships.
Policy guides decisions toward that purpose.
Character is reflected in consistent behavior.
Use an engineering case with stakeholders, consequences and a justified action.
topics.question: A software intern finds a data leak before a demo. Explain an ethical response.
steps: Identify affected people: users, teammates and the organization.
Apply values of trust and responsibility: protect users and report facts honestly.
Choose a policy: inform the responsible team, restrict exposure and fix the cause.
Show character by following through, testing the repair and avoiding a false claim that the issue is resolved.
topics.mcq: Which action best demonstrates professional responsibility?
options: Hide the leak until after the demo
Report, contain and verify a fix
topics.explanation: Responsible conduct protects affected people and communicates truthfully.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Humanistic education & professional ethics
topics.brief: Humanistic education joins technical competence with right understanding and responsible participation in society and nature.
topics.hinglish: Engineer ka answer sirf “works” nahi; kis par kya impact hoga, ye bhi important hai.
points: Technical skill helps implement a solution; ethical understanding guides its purpose and use.
Evaluate usefulness, fairness, environmental impact and long-term consequences.
Use people-friendly and environmentally responsible technology examples.
For a long answer: define, explain the relationship, give an example and conclude with a practical action.
topics.question: Explain how a campus energy project can reflect professional ethics.
steps: Define the aim: meet genuine energy needs with responsible resource use.
Apply competence: measure consumption and design an efficient solution.
Consider people: accessibility, affordability, maintenance responsibilities and transparent data.
Evaluate environmental effects and monitor results; education should develop both the technical ability and judgment to do this.
topics.mcq: Humanistic education aims to combine:
options: Skills with right understanding and responsibility
topics.explanation: The syllabus connects professional competence with humane purpose and conduct.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Value education & self-exploration
topics.brief: Value education examines what is valuable and how to live with understanding, relationships and adequate physical facilities.
topics.hinglish: Happiness aur physical facility related hain, lekin same cheez nahi.
points: The course method is self-exploration: examine a proposal and validate it in living.
Natural acceptance is distinguished from temporary preference and external pressure.
Human aspiration includes continuous happiness and prosperity; prosperity concerns assurance of sufficient physical facilities.
Right understanding guides relationships and the use of resources; examine the present situation through these priorities.
topics.question: Distinguish happiness and prosperity with a student example.
steps: Happiness concerns harmony and fulfilment in the self and relationships.
Prosperity concerns a sense of having sufficient physical resources for needs.
A laptop and books support study, while trust and meaningful learning contribute differently.
More possessions alone do not establish harmonious relationships or clarity of purpose.
topics.mcq: In UHV, self-exploration means:
topics.explanation: It involves personal verification and experiential validation.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Self, body, sanyam & health
topics.brief: UHV distinguishes the conscious self from the body and examines harmony between them.
topics.hinglish: Body ki physical needs limited; self ko right understanding aur feelings chahiye.
points: The body is treated as an instrument of the self; identify needs, activities and responses of each.
The self has activities such as desire, thought and expectation in this framework.
Sanyam means responsibility for nurturing, protecting and rightly using the body.
Health requires a suitable routine, nourishment, rest and physical activity; this is a course framework, not individualized medical treatment.
topics.question: Explain harmony between self and body during exam preparation.
steps: Identify the self’s purpose: learning with clarity rather than uncontrolled comparison.
Identify bodily needs: meals, sleep, movement and a workable environment.
Plan study and rest so the body supports the chosen purpose.
Review habits and consequences; responsible regulation is more than suppressing needs.
topics.mcq: Sanyam in this course emphasizes:
options: Responsibility for nurturing and using the body
topics.explanation: The emphasis is responsible self-regulation in relation to the body.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Relationships, justice & social harmony
topics.brief: Harmony in family and society builds on understanding relationships and fulfilling values consistently.
topics.hinglish: Trust intention se related hai; competence ki kami ko bad intention mat samjho.
points: Study trust, respect, affection, care, guidance, reverence, glory, gratitude and love.
Distinguish intention from competence; help improve competence without assuming hostile intention.
Respect involves right evaluation, not discrimination by wealth, position or physical attributes.
Justice and fulfilment in relationships support resolution, prosperity, fearlessness and co-existence at social level.
topics.question: A teammate misses a task because they lack the skill. Apply intention versus competence.
steps: Ask what they intended and what they were able to do; these are separate questions.
Do not infer malicious intent solely from a poor result.
Provide support, a realistic responsibility and a review process.
Maintain accountability while building competence and trust.
topics.mcq: Poor competence necessarily proves bad intention:
topics.explanation: The framework asks us to distinguish the two.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Humanistic constitution & universal order
topics.brief: The course imagines social arrangements that support human development and mutually fulfilling relationships.
topics.hinglish: Constitution yahan sirf legal articles yaad karna nahi; humane social principles samajhna hai.
points: Humanistic education develops right understanding and professional competence together.
A humanistic constitution, in this framework, expresses shared principles of justice, responsibility and participation.
Universal human order extends harmony from individual and family to society and nature.
Evaluate institutions through education, health/self-regulation, production, exchange and justice rather than slogans alone.
topics.question: How can a college support a humanistic social order?
steps: Education combines technical learning with reflection and responsibility.
Transparent processes provide fairness in assessment and access to support.
Resource use, production and waste handling consider environmental effects.
Students and staff practise participation, trust, dispute resolution and accountability.
topics.mcq: Humanistic education should develop:
topics.explanation: The framework joins purpose and capability.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
topics.title: Transition to universal human order
topics.brief: Transition is a sustained process of personal understanding, responsible conduct and institutional change.
topics.hinglish: Individual action aur social systems dono levels par change chahiye.
points: At individual level: self-exploration, competence, ethical work and responsible relationships.
At family/community level: dialogue, mutual support and fair processes.
At societal level: institutions that support education, justice and sustainable production.
Use measurable, realistic steps and case studies; do not claim one campaign instantly transforms society.
topics.question: Propose a transition plan for an unethical software workplace.
steps: Individuals learn secure engineering, report issues honestly and protect users.
Teams agree on review standards, responsible escalation and transparent records.
Management aligns incentives with user well-being and verified quality.
Review outcomes and correct failures; transformation requires sustained individual and institutional effort.
topics.mcq: A durable transition requires:
topics.explanation: Both levels reinforce responsible behavior.

units.text: Introduction - Value Education Universal human values; self exploration, natural acceptance an experimental validation; Human aspirations, right understanding, relationship and physical facility, current scenario; Understanding and living in harmony at various levels.
units.title: Module 1

units.text: Harmony in the Nature and Existence Harmony in the nature. Four orders of nature; existence as co-existence, harmony at all levels of existence.

units.title: Module 5

subject.name: Python Programming Lab
subject.description: Runnable programs, algorithms, file handling and scientific Python.

resources: Language basics, data structures, exceptions and files
Web routes; run a Flask server on your computer, outside this browser lab

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
topics.title: Interpreter, scripts & indentation
topics.brief: Python can execute interactive statements or a saved .py script. Indentation defines suites of statements.
topics.hinglish: Colon ke baad block indent karo; tabs aur spaces mix mat karo.
points: REPL is useful for small experiments; scripts save a repeatable sequence of instructions.
Use consistent four-space indentation for a block.
IndentationError is a syntax-related error; correct structure before reasoning about output.
Practice input/output, numeric conversion and distinguishing strings from numbers.
topics.recall: if condition: followed by an indented suite
topics.question: Demonstrate an indentation error and its correction.
steps: A line such as if True: requires an indented body.
The string "if True:\nprint(1)" is incorrectly indented.
The example catches the deliberate IndentationError during exec.
The corrected block indents print(1) and runs successfully.
topics.mcq: What defines a Python block?
topics.explanation: Indentation is part of Python syntax.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
topics.title: Distance & command-line addition
topics.brief: Read values explicitly and convert text to numbers before arithmetic.
topics.hinglish: input() aur sys.argv text dete hain; number conversion zaroori hai.
points: Distance between points is sqrt((x2−x1)²+(y2−y1)²).
math.hypot(dx,dy) computes this conveniently.
sys.argv[0] is the script name; subsequent items are command-line arguments.
Validate the argument count and numeric input; strings concatenate if you add them without conversion.
topics.question: Find the distance between (1,2) and (4,6), and outline add.py.
steps: Coordinate differences are 3 and 4.
Distance=sqrt(9+16)=5.
For add.py, require exactly two user arguments.
Convert them to float and print the sum; report invalid input.
topics.mcq: sys.argv[0] normally contains:
topics.explanation: User arguments begin at index 1.
topics.code:
# distance.py
from math import hypot
def distance(x1, y1, x2, y2):
    return hypot(x2-x1, y2-y1)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    x1, y1 = map(float, input("Point 1 (x y): ").split())
    x2, y2 = map(float, input("Point 2 (x y): ").split())
    print(distance(x1, y1, x2, y2))

# Save the following part separately as add.py:
# import sys
# if len(sys.argv) != 3:
#     raise SystemExit("Usage: python add.py NUMBER NUMBER")
# try:
#     print(float(sys.argv[1]) + float(sys.argv[2]))
# except ValueError:
#     raise SystemExit("Both arguments must be numeric")

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
topics.title: Even numbers, loops & countdown
topics.brief: Control flow chooses actions and repeats statements. range excludes its stop value.
topics.hinglish: 1/2 se 1/10 tak loop ke liye range(2,11), range(2,10) nahi.
points: n%2==0 tests evenness for positive, zero and negative integers.
Use for with a range or a sequence; each item is visited in order.
Use while when repetition depends on a changing condition.
A countdown needs an update so the loop terminates; define behavior for a negative start.
topics.question: Print 1/2 through 1/10 and count down from 3 to 0.
steps: Loop denominator d over range(2,11) and print 1/d.
For a countdown, initialize n=3.
While n≥0, print n and reduce n by one.
The countdown output is 3,2,1,0 and the loop then terminates.
topics.mcq: list(range(2,5)) gives:
topics.explanation: The stop value 5 is excluded.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
topics.title: Prime/Fibonacci sums, search & sort
topics.brief: Use efficient algorithms and state boundary conditions before coding.
topics.hinglish: Below 2 million exclusive; Fibonacci values not exceeding 4 million inclusive.
points: A sieve avoids repeated primality tests when summing primes below 2,000,000.
Fibonacci starts 1,2 here; sum even terms ≤4,000,000.
Binary search requires sorted input; linear search does not.
Implement selection and insertion sort and trace their passes, not just a built-in sorted call.
topics.question: How would you compute both large sums efficiently and verify them?
steps: Initialize a sieve with 0 and 1 nonprime; strike multiples from p².
Sum marked indices below 2,000,000 → 142913828922.
Generate Fibonacci pairs (a,b) starting at (1,2), adding a only if even and ≤4,000,000.
The second sum is 4613732. Test smaller limits first to catch off-by-one errors.
topics.mcq: Binary search requires its input sequence to be:
topics.explanation: Sorted order justifies discarding half the search range.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
topics.title: Character dictionaries, split/join & birthdays
topics.brief: Dictionaries map unique keys to values and support efficient lookup.
topics.hinglish: Character frequency mein har occurrence count hota hai, space bhi agar filter na karo.
points: Use dict.get(character,0)+1 or collections.Counter for counts.
split turns text into tokens; separator.join(tokens) builds a string.
Store birthday lookup data as name→date strings and handle missing names explicitly.
Lists and tuples are ordered; sets remove duplicates; dictionaries map keys to values.
topics.question: Count characters in "banana" and explain split/join.
steps: Read each character and increment its dictionary entry.
Final frequencies are b:1,a:3,n:2.
"exam prep".split() produces ["exam","prep"].
"-".join(those tokens) produces "exam-prep".
topics.mcq: Which expression safely increments a missing character count?
topics.explanation: get supplies the initial zero.

topics.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
topics.title: Combine lists & file character frequency
topics.brief: Combine keys and values carefully; frequency analysis summarizes content but does not reliably identify its programming language.
topics.hinglish: zip shorter input par stop karta hai; equal length requirement check karo.
points: dict(zip(keys,values)) combines aligned pairs; duplicate keys overwrite earlier values.

steps: Inserting r in "cat" produces "cart", so one edit suffices.

topics.code:
from collections import Counter

def nearly_equal(a, b):
    if abs(len(a)-len(b)) > 1: return False
    if len(a) > len(b): a, b = b, a
    i = j = edits = 0
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if a[i] == b[j]:
            i += 1; j += 1
        else:
            edits += 1
            if edits > 1: return False
            if len(a) == len(b): i += 1
            j += 1
    edits += (len(a)-i) + (len(b)-j)
    return edits == 1

def dups(values):
    counts = Counter(values)
    return [x for x in counts if counts[x] > 1]

def unique(values):
    return list(dict.fromkeys(values))
# These list helpers require hashable elements.
print(nearly_equal("cat", "cart"))
print(dups([1,2,1,3,2]))
print(unique([1,2,1,3,2]))

topics.mcq: The initial accumulator for a product is:
topics.explanation: 1 is the multiplicative identity.
topics.code:
def cumulative_product(values):
    result, product = [], 1
    for x in values:
        product *= x
        result.append(product)
    return result

def reverse(values):
    return [values[i] for i in range(len(values)-1, -1, -1)]

gcd = lambda a, b: abs(a) if b == 0 else gcd(b, a % b)
lcm = lambda a, b: 0 if a == 0 or b == 0 else abs(a // gcd(a,b) * b)

print(cumulative_product([2,3,4]))
print(reverse([2,3,4]))
print(gcd(12,18), lcm(12,18))

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: Canonical SOP from an expression
chapterQuestions.prompt: Write F(A,B,C)=A+B′C as a sum of minterms, using ABC as the bit order.
steps: List assignments with A=1: 100,101,110,111. These contribute minterms 4,5,6,7.
For A=0, the term B′C is 1 only at 001, contributing minterm 1.
Take the union of the assignments; do not count 101 twice.
Therefore F=Σm(1,4,5,6,7)=A′B′C+AB′C′+AB′C+ABC′+ABC.
chapterQuestions.trap: State the variable order before converting a binary assignment to a minterm number.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: Four-variable K-map with XNOR recognition
chapterQuestions.prompt: Minimise F(A,B,C,D)=Σm(0,2,5,7,8,10,13,15) using a K-map. Give a two-level expression and a compact gate implementation.
steps: Use rows AB=00,01,11,10 and columns CD=00,01,11,10. This Gray order makes adjacent cells differ in one bit.
Enter 1 in exactly the eight listed cells. Keep the remaining cells 0; no don’t-care terms are supplied.
Group {0,2,8,10}. The wraparound group has B=0 and D=0; A and C vary, so it gives B′D′.
Group {5,7,13,15}. It has B=1 and D=1 while A and C vary, giving BD.
The minimal SOP is F=B′D′+BD. Every supplied minterm belongs to one of these groups and no 0-cell is covered.
This is the equality function of B and D: F=NOT(B XOR D). One two-input XNOR gate implements it; A and C are unused.
Check B,D=00,01,10,11: outputs are 1,0,0,1. This reproduces the original minterm set for both values of A and C.
chapterQuestions.answer: F=B′D′+BD=B XNOR D
chapterQuestions.trap: K-map edges wrap around. Never use ordinary binary order 00,01,10,11 for adjacent rows or columns.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: Correct a BCD addition
chapterQuestions.prompt: Add BCD digits 9 and 8 and show the correction.
steps: Write the inputs as 1001 and 1000.
Binary addition gives 1 0001. A carry out means a BCD correction is required.
Add 0110 to the low four-bit sum: 0001+0110=0111; retain the decimal carry 1.
The BCD result is 0001 0111, representing decimal 17.
chapterQuestions.trap: Do not read the uncorrected low nibble 0001 as the final units digit.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: Implement a Boolean function with a multiplexer
chapterQuestions.prompt: Implement F(A,B,C)=Σm(1,2,6,7) using one 4:1 multiplexer with select lines S1=A and S0=B. Verify every input case.
steps: Partition the truth table by AB. For each pair, compare the required outputs for C=0 and C=1.
For AB=00, minterms 0 and 1 have outputs 0 and 1; connect I0=C.
For AB=01, minterms 2 and 3 have outputs 1 and 0; connect I1=C′ using an inverter.
For AB=10, minterms 4 and 5 both give 0; tie I2 to logic 0.
For AB=11, minterms 6 and 7 both give 1; tie I3 to logic 1. Connect the MUX output to F.
The MUX equation becomes F=A′B′C+A′BC′+AB. In ascending ABC order 000..111, the outputs are 0,1,1,0,0,0,1,1.
Only indices 1,2,6,7 are high, confirming the implementation. A 4:1 MUX chooses one of four data inputs; its select lines are not extra data inputs.
chapterQuestions.trap: Keep S1 and S0 in the stated order; swapping them swaps the I1 and I2 cases.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: JK flip-flop state trace
chapterQuestions.prompt: An edge-triggered JK flip-flop starts at Q=0. At four successive active edges, JK is 10,11,00,01. Find Q after every edge.
steps: JK=10 sets Q, so after edge 1 the state is 1.
JK=11 toggles the stored state, giving Q=0 after edge 2.
JK=00 holds the state, so Q remains 0 after edge 3.
JK=01 resets the state, giving Q=0 after edge 4.
chapterQuestions.answer: Q after the four edges: 1,0,0,0
chapterQuestions.trap: For an edge-triggered flip-flop, apply the input pair at the active edge, not continuously.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: Design a synchronous modulo-4 counter
chapterQuestions.prompt: Design a two-bit synchronous binary up counter using D flip-flops. Derive next-state equations, give a state trace and identify output frequencies for a 1 kHz clock.
steps: Use two state bits Q1,Q0 and the sequence 00→01→10→11→00. Two flip-flops are enough because 2²=4 states.
For a D flip-flop, D equals the required next value of Q. The table is current 00: next 01; 01:10; 10:11; 11:00.
Q0 changes on every clock, so D0=NOT Q0.
Q1 changes exactly when the current Q0 is 1. Its next-state column is 0,1,1,0, giving D1=Q1 XOR Q0.
Wire both flip-flops to the same active clock edge. Feed an inverter from Q0 to D0 and an XOR of Q1,Q0 to D1. Reset both state bits to 0.
Starting from reset, states after clock edges 1..8 are 01,10,11,00,01,10,11,00. Every possible two-bit state is used.
At a 1 kHz input clock, Q0 completes one cycle in two clock periods: 500 Hz. Q1 completes one in four: 250 Hz. These values assume ideal synchronous operation after reset.
chapterQuestions.answer: D0=Q0′; D1=Q1 XOR Q0; Q0=500 Hz, Q1=250 Hz
chapterQuestions.trap: Do not clock the second flip-flop from Q0: that would produce a ripple counter rather than the specified synchronous design.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: Address and data lines for memory
chapterQuestions.prompt: A memory stores 8K words of 16 bits. How many address lines and data lines are required, and what is its capacity in bytes?
steps: Interpret 8K as 8×1024=8192=2¹³ words.
Address lines select a word, so 13 address lines are required.
Each word is 16 bits, so there are 16 data lines for a parallel word interface.
Capacity is 8192×16=131072 bits=16384 bytes=16 KiB.
chapterQuestions.answer: 13 address lines, 16 data lines, 16 KiB
chapterQuestions.trap: Count words, not bits, when calculating the number of address lines.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: Memory expansion with decoder selection
chapterQuestions.prompt: Build a 16K×8 memory using 4K×4 memory chips. Find the number of chips, address connections and decoder size; explain the selected chips at address 0x2ABC.
steps: A 4K×4 chip supplies 4096 words of four bits. Two chips in parallel provide one 4K×8 bank: one chip carries D0..D3 and the other D4..D7.
The required depth is 16K/4K=4 banks. Therefore use 4×2=8 chips. Check capacity: 8×4096×4=131072 bits, equal to 16384×8.
The system needs 14 address lines because 16K=2¹⁴. Connect A0..A11 to every chip to select one of its 4096 local words.
Use A13,A12 as inputs to a 2-to-4 decoder. Each decoder output enables both chips in one bank. Chip-select polarity must match the devices; invert decoder outputs if needed.
Connect common read/output-enable and write-enable controls appropriately. During a read, enable only the selected bank so unselected outputs do not contend on the shared bus.
For address 0x2ABC, the bank number is floor(0x2ABC/0x1000)=2, corresponding to A13A12=10. The local address is 0xABC=2748.
Thus the two chips of bank 2 jointly supply one eight-bit word at local word 2748. The bank ranges are 0x0000–0x0FFF, 0x1000–0x1FFF, 0x2000–0x2FFF and 0x3000–0x3FFF.
chapterQuestions.answer: 8 chips arranged as four 4K×8 banks; address 0x2ABC selects bank 2, offset 0xABC
chapterQuestions.trap: Width expansion and depth expansion are separate steps. A decoder chooses a bank, not an individual bit chip within the bank.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: Signal assignment versus variable assignment
chapterQuestions.prompt: In a VHDL process, distinguish signal assignment <= from variable assignment :=. What does this process do: process(a) variable v: std_logic; begin v := a; y <= v; end process;?
steps: A variable assignment uses := and updates the variable immediately within the current process execution.
A signal assignment uses <= and schedules an update; later statements in the same process do not necessarily see that new signal value immediately.
Here v receives a immediately, and y is then scheduled to receive that same value.
The process models a combinational connection y=a; process(a) is sensitive to its only read signal.
chapterQuestions.answer: v updates immediately; y is scheduled to follow a
chapterQuestions.trap: Do not replace v with a signal and assume a later statement in the same process sees the newly scheduled value.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
chapterQuestions.title: VHDL synchronous counter with a test trace
chapterQuestions.prompt: Write a synthesizable two-bit VHDL counter with a rising-edge clock and synchronous active-high reset. Explain the output sequence for reset values 1,0,0,0,0 at five clock edges.
steps: Use IEEE std_logic_1164 and numeric_std. An unsigned state register permits defined numeric addition without nonstandard arithmetic packages.
Entity: entity counter2 is port(clk,rst: in std_logic; q: out std_logic_vector(1 downto 0)); end entity;

Architecture: architecture rtl of counter2 is signal count: unsigned(1 downto 0); begin process(clk) begin if rising_edge(clk) then if rst='1' then count <= "00"; else count <= count + 1; end if; end if; end process; q <= std_logic_vector(count); end architecture;
All register updates are inside rising_edge(clk), so this describes two clocked storage bits. Reset is tested inside that edge condition, making it synchronous.
At the five specified edges the outputs are 00,01,10,11,00. Addition wraps modulo 4 because the state is only two bits wide.

In a testbench, apply reset before the first edge and change inputs away from active edges. Check q after the clocked signal updates have settled, rather than in the same simulation delta as the edge.

Synthesis creates a register plus increment/reset logic. Simulation establishes behavior for tested stimulus; synthesis alone does not prove the expected sequence. Before the first reset edge the uninitialised register is not guaranteed to be 00.
chapterQuestions.answer: Clock-edge sequence: 00,01,10,11,00
chapterQuestions.trap: Reset outside rising_edge(clk) would be asynchronous, changing the specification.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:cpp
chapterQuestions.title: Reference alias versus object copy
chapterQuestions.prompt: Given int a=5; int& r=a; int b=a; r+=2; b+=10;, find a,r,b and explain why.
steps: At declaration, r is an alias for a; it does not create a separate int object.
b is a separate int initialised with a copy of the value 5.
r+=2 changes a itself to 7, so reading r also gives 7.
b+=10 changes only b to 15. Final values are a=7,r=7,b=15.
chapterQuestions.trap: A reference declaration is not a copy operation. Later assignment through r changes its referent.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:cpp
chapterQuestions.title: Objects through arrays, pointers and references
chapterQuestions.prompt: Trace the following object operations and supply a complete C++ program: create Counter objects with values 3 and 7; add 2 to the first through a reference; add 4 to the second through a pointer; copy the first and add 10 only to the copy.
steps: Encapsulate the integer so clients change it through a method: class Counter { int value; public: explicit Counter(int v=0):value(v){} void add(int n){this->value+=n;} int get() const{return value;} };
Define void bump(Counter& c){c.add(2);} . The reference parameter refers to the caller’s object, so the update persists after the function returns.
In main, declare Counter a[2]={Counter(3),Counter(7)}; Counter* p=a; bump(*p); (p+1)->add(4); . Array elements are contiguous; p+1 points to the second object.
After these calls a[0] holds 5 and a[1] holds 11. The this pointer inside add identifies the particular object receiving the call.
Execute Counter copy=a[0]; copy.add(10); . The compiler-generated copy constructor copies the int member. copy becomes 15 while a[0] stays 5.

Complete the program with #include <iostream> and int main(){Counter a[2]={Counter(3),Counter(7)}; Counter* p=a; bump(*p); (p+1)->add(4); Counter copy=a[0]; copy.add(10); std::cout<<a[0].get()<<" "<<a[1].get()<<" "<<copy.get()<<"\n";} after the class and bump definition.
The output is 5 11 15. Objects use automatic storage, so no new/delete is needed. Never dereference p+2, which is the one-past-end pointer.
chapterQuestions.trap: Passing Counter by value to bump would modify a temporary copy instead of the original.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:cpp
chapterQuestions.title: Resolve overloaded calls
chapterQuestions.prompt: Two functions are declared: void f(int); void f(double);. Which overload is selected by f(5), f(5.5) and f('A')?
steps: The literal 5 has type int, so f(int) is an exact match.
The literal 5.5 has type double, so f(double) is an exact match.
The char argument in f('A') can undergo integral promotion to int; conversion to double is a lower-ranked conversion.
Therefore f('A') selects f(int). The selection depends on types and conversion ranking, not on the printed appearance of a value.
chapterQuestions.answer: f(int), f(double), f(int)
chapterQuestions.trap: Return type alone cannot distinguish overloaded functions with otherwise identical parameter lists.

chapterQuestions.subject: cia-2-2025-26:cpp
chapterQuestions.title: Complex addition with constructor and operator overloading
chapterQuestions.prompt: Implement a Complex class supporting default/parameterised construction, copying and c=a+b. For a=(2,3) and b=(4,−5), print c and a copy of c after adding (1,1) only to that copy.
steps: Store real and imaginary components as two private doubles. A constructor with defaults Complex(double r=0,double i=0):re(r),im(i){} covers both the default and parameterised cases.
Define the copy constructor as Complex(const Complex&)=default;. Since the members are values and own no external resource, memberwise copying is appropriate.
Define Complex operator+(const Complex& rhs) const {return Complex(re+rhs.re,im+rhs.im);} . The const qualifiers allow reading both operands without changing either.

A complete class body is: class Complex {double re,im; public: Complex(double r=0,double i=0):re(r),im(i){} Complex(const Complex&)=default; Complex operator+(const Complex& x) const{return {re+x.re,im+x.im};} void print() const{std::cout<<"("<<re<<","<<im<<")\n";} };
