long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
long.title: Memory expansion with decoder selection
long.prompt: Build a 16K×8 memory using 4K×4 memory chips. Find the number of chips, address connections and decoder size; explain the selected chips at address 0x2ABC.
steps: A 4K×4 chip supplies 4096 words of four bits. Two chips in parallel provide one 4K×8 bank: one chip carries D0..D3 and the other D4..D7.
The required depth is 16K/4K=4 banks. Therefore use 4×2=8 chips. Check capacity: 8×4096×4=131072 bits, equal to 16384×8.
The system needs 14 address lines because 16K=2¹⁴. Connect A0..A11 to every chip to select one of its 4096 local words.
Use A13,A12 as inputs to a 2-to-4 decoder. Each decoder output enables both chips in one bank. Chip-select polarity must match the devices; invert decoder outputs if needed.
Connect common read/output-enable and write-enable controls appropriately. During a read, enable only the selected bank so unselected outputs do not contend on the shared bus.
For address 0x2ABC, the bank number is floor(0x2ABC/0x1000)=2, corresponding to A13A12=10. The local address is 0xABC=2748.
Thus the two chips of bank 2 jointly supply one eight-bit word at local word 2748. The bank ranges are 0x0000–0x0FFF, 0x1000–0x1FFF, 0x2000–0x2FFF and 0x3000–0x3FFF.
long.answer: 8 chips arranged as four 4K×8 banks; address 0x2ABC selects bank 2, offset 0xABC
long.trap: Width expansion and depth expansion are separate steps. A decoder chooses a bank, not an individual bit chip within the bank.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:de
long.title: VHDL synchronous counter with a test trace
long.prompt: Write a synthesizable two-bit VHDL counter with a rising-edge clock and synchronous active-high reset. Explain the output sequence for reset values 1,0,0,0,0 at five clock edges.
steps: Use IEEE std_logic_1164 and numeric_std. An unsigned state register permits defined numeric addition without nonstandard arithmetic packages.
Entity: entity counter2 is port(clk,rst: in std_logic; q: out std_logic_vector(1 downto 0)); end entity;

Architecture: architecture rtl of counter2 is signal count: unsigned(1 downto 0); begin process(clk) begin if rising_edge(clk) then if rst='1' then count <= "00"; else count <= count + 1; end if; end if; end process; q <= std_logic_vector(count); end architecture;
All register updates are inside rising_edge(clk), so this describes two clocked storage bits. Reset is tested inside that edge condition, making it synchronous.
At the five specified edges the outputs are 00,01,10,11,00. Addition wraps modulo 4 because the state is only two bits wide.

In a testbench, apply reset before the first edge and change inputs away from active edges. Check q after the clocked signal updates have settled, rather than in the same simulation delta as the edge.

Synthesis creates a register plus increment/reset logic. Simulation establishes behavior for tested stimulus; synthesis alone does not prove the expected sequence. Before the first reset edge the uninitialised register is not guaranteed to be 00.
long.answer: Clock-edge sequence: 00,01,10,11,00
long.trap: Reset outside rising_edge(clk) would be asynchronous, changing the specification.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:cpp
long.title: Objects through arrays, pointers and references
long.prompt: Trace the following object operations and supply a complete C++ program: create Counter objects with values 3 and 7; add 2 to the first through a reference; add 4 to the second through a pointer; copy the first and add 10 only to the copy.
steps: Encapsulate the integer so clients change it through a method: class Counter { int value; public: explicit Counter(int v=0):value(v){} void add(int n){this->value+=n;} int get() const{return value;} };
Define void bump(Counter& c){c.add(2);} . The reference parameter refers to the caller’s object, so the update persists after the function returns.
In main, declare Counter a[2]={Counter(3),Counter(7)}; Counter* p=a; bump(*p); (p+1)->add(4); . Array elements are contiguous; p+1 points to the second object.
After these calls a[0] holds 5 and a[1] holds 11. The this pointer inside add identifies the particular object receiving the call.
Execute Counter copy=a[0]; copy.add(10); . The compiler-generated copy constructor copies the int member. copy becomes 15 while a[0] stays 5.

Complete the program with #include <iostream> and int main(){Counter a[2]={Counter(3),Counter(7)}; Counter* p=a; bump(*p); (p+1)->add(4); Counter copy=a[0]; copy.add(10); std::cout<<a[0].get()<<" "<<a[1].get()<<" "<<copy.get()<<"\n";} after the class and bump definition.
The output is 5 11 15. Objects use automatic storage, so no new/delete is needed. Never dereference p+2, which is the one-past-end pointer.
long.trap: Passing Counter by value to bump would modify a temporary copy instead of the original.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:cpp
long.title: Complex addition with constructor and operator overloading
long.prompt: Implement a Complex class supporting default/parameterised construction, copying and c=a+b. For a=(2,3) and b=(4,−5), print c and a copy of c after adding (1,1) only to that copy.
steps: Store real and imaginary components as two private doubles. A constructor with defaults Complex(double r=0,double i=0):re(r),im(i){} covers both the default and parameterised cases.
Define the copy constructor as Complex(const Complex&)=default;. Since the members are values and own no external resource, memberwise copying is appropriate.
Define Complex operator+(const Complex& rhs) const {return Complex(re+rhs.re,im+rhs.im);} . The const qualifiers allow reading both operands without changing either.

A complete class body is: class Complex {double re,im; public: Complex(double r=0,double i=0):re(r),im(i){} Complex(const Complex&)=default; Complex operator+(const Complex& x) const{return {re+x.re,im+x.im};} void print() const{std::cout<<"("<<re<<","<<im<<")\n";} };
After #include <iostream> and the class, use int main(){Complex a(2,3),b(4,-5); Complex c=a+b; Complex d=c; d=d+Complex(1,1); c.print(); d.print();}.
Componentwise addition gives c=(2+4,3−5)=(6,−2). d starts as (6,−2), then changes to (7,−1). c remains unchanged.
The output is (6,-2) on the first line and (7,-1) on the second. Binary member operator+ has one explicit parameter because the left operand is the implicit this object.
long.answer: c=(6,−2); modified copy d=(7,−1)
long.trap: Do not return a reference to a local Complex object created inside operator+; return by value.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:cpp
long.title: Abstract classes, dispatch and checked downcasting
long.prompt: Create abstract Shape and derived Square and Rectangle classes. Use base pointers to obtain areas for side 3 and sides 2,5. Demonstrate a successful and a failed dynamic_cast to Square*.
steps: Define an abstract interface: struct Shape { virtual double area() const=0; virtual ~Shape()=default; };. The pure virtual area function prevents direct Shape objects and provides dynamic dispatch.

Define struct Square:Shape {double side; explicit Square(double x):side(x){} double area() const override{return side*side;} }; and struct Rectangle:Shape {double w,h; Rectangle(double a,double b):w(a),h(b){} double area() const override{return w*h;} };.
In main, create Square sq(3); Rectangle rect(2,5); Shape* p=&sq; Shape* q=▭. The pointers are non-owning references to automatic objects, so do not delete them.
Calls p->area() and q->area() are resolved using the dynamic object types. They return 9 and 10, despite both pointers having static type Shape*.
auto a=dynamic_cast<Square*>(p); succeeds and a points to sq. auto b=dynamic_cast<Square*>(q); fails and yields nullptr because a Rectangle is not a Square.
With #include <iostream>, print std::cout<<p->area()<<" "<<q->area()<<"\n"; std::cout<<std::boolalpha<<(a!=nullptr)<<" "<<(b!=nullptr)<<"\n";. Output is 9 10, then true false.
The base is polymorphic because it has virtual functions, enabling these checked downcasts. A failed pointer dynamic_cast returns nullptr; a failed reference dynamic_cast throws std::bad_cast.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:cpp
long.title: A checked generic array accessor
long.prompt: Write a function template checked_at that accepts a built-in array by reference, deduces its size and throws std::out_of_range for an invalid index. Trace modifying index 1 of {4,8,12} to 9 and then reading index 3.
steps: Include <iostream>, <stdexcept> and <cstddef>. The template needs both an element type T and a non-type size parameter N.

Define template<class T,std::size_t N> T& checked_at(T (&a)[N],std::size_t i){if(i>=N)throw std::out_of_range("index outside array");return a[i];}. Passing the array by reference preserves its size for deduction.
Returning T& permits assignment through the returned reference. For int a[]={4,8,12}, deduction gives T=int and N=3.

In main, execute int a[]={4,8,12}; try{checked_at(a,1)=9; std::cout<<checked_at(a,1)<<"
"; std::cout<<checked_at(a,3)<<"
";}catch(const std::out_of_range& e){std::cout<<e.what()<<"
";}.
The first access is valid and changes the second element from 8 to 9. The next statement prints 9.
Index 3 fails i>=N because valid indices are 0,1,2. The throw transfers control to the matching handler; the attempted array read never occurs.

The complete output is 9 followed by index outside array. The final array is {4,9,12}. The same template works for a double array; an index parameter of size_t cannot represent a meaningful negative index, so caller input should be validated before conversion.

long.trap: Use i>=N, not i>N. The index equal to the length is already out of bounds.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:cpp
long.title: Formatted streams and STL list processing
long.prompt: Read the integers from the text "40 10 30 10" into std::list<int>, sort them, remove duplicate adjacent values, calculate the mean and print it with two decimal places.
steps: Include <iostream>, <sstream>, <list>, <numeric> and <iomanip>. Create std::istringstream in("40 10 30 10"); std::list<int> values; int x; while(in>>x) values.push_back(x);.
Use values.sort();. Unlike vector, list does not provide random-access iterators, so std::sort is not the appropriate algorithm for its iterators.
After sorting the list is 10,10,30,40. Call values.unique(); to remove consecutive equal values. The result is 10,30,40.
Compute int total=std::accumulate(values.begin(),values.end(),0);. The sum is 80 and the size is 3. Reject an empty list before dividing by its size.
Compute double mean=static_cast<double>(total)/values.size();. Converting before division avoids integer truncation; the mean is 26.6666….
Print each element with for(int v:values)std::cout<<v<<" "; then std::cout<<"\n"<<std::fixed<<std::setprecision(2)<<mean<<"\n";. The displayed mean is 26.67.
All names are qualified with std::, so no global using-directive is needed. unique removes adjacent duplicates only, which is why sorting precedes it in this task.
long.answer: Sorted distinct values: 10 30 40; sum 80; displayed mean 26.67.
long.trap: setprecision(2) alone means significant digits by default; combine it with fixed for two digits after the decimal point.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
long.title: Equivalence classes and a quotient set
long.prompt: On S={0,1,…,11}, define aRb if 4 divides a−b. Prove R is an equivalence relation, list its classes and count its ordered pairs.
steps: Reflexivity: a−a=0 and 4 divides 0, so every a is related to itself.
Symmetry: if a−b=4k then b−a=4(−k), so aRb implies bRa.
Transitivity: if a−b=4k and b−c=4m, then a−c=4(k+m), hence aRc. The three properties prove equivalence.
Group elements by their remainder modulo 4. The classes are [0]={0,4,8}, [1]={1,5,9}, [2]={2,6,10}, [3]={3,7,11}.
These four classes are disjoint and their union is S, so they form the partition associated with R. The quotient set S/R contains these four sets as its elements.
Within each three-element class, every ordered pair is related, including self-pairs: 3×3=9 pairs. Different classes have no related pairs.
The total is 4×9=36 ordered pairs. This counts direction separately: for example, (0,4) and (4,0) are different ordered pairs.
long.answer: Four equivalence classes; |S/R|=4; |R|=36.
long.trap: A quotient set contains equivalence classes, not a new list of all twelve original integers.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
long.title: Divisor lattice of 12
long.prompt: For D={1,2,3,4,6,12} ordered by divisibility, give the Hasse covers, meet/join of 4 and 6, and all complementary pairs. Is the lattice complemented?
steps: The order a≤b means a divides b. Reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity follow from divisibility of positive integers, so D is a poset.
The Hasse covering pairs are (1,2),(1,3),(2,4),(2,6),(3,6),(4,12),(6,12). Draw 1 at the bottom and 12 at the top; omit transitive edges such as 1→6.
Every pair has a greatest common divisor and least common multiple within D. Therefore meet is gcd and join is lcm, so this poset is a lattice.
For 4 and 6, the meet is gcd(4,6)=2, and the join is lcm(4,6)=12.
The least element is 1 and greatest is 12. Complementary elements x,y must satisfy gcd(x,y)=1 and lcm(x,y)=12 simultaneously.
The complementary pairs are 1 with 12 and 3 with 4. Element 2 has no complement: only 1 and 3 in D are coprime to 2, and their lcm with 2 is at most 6. Element 6 also has none.
Hence this bounded lattice is not complemented. It is distributive: divisors of 12=2²×3 correspond to exponent pairs (i,j), with 0≤i≤2 and 0≤j≤1; meet and join act componentwise as min and max.
long.answer: 4∧6=2, 4∨6=12; complements 1↔12 and 3↔4; not complemented.
long.trap: A lattice can have some complements without every element having one.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
long.title: Solve a recurrence using a generating function
long.prompt: Solve aₙ=3aₙ₋₁+2 for n≥1, with a₀=1, using an ordinary generating function. Verify the first four terms.
steps: Define A(x)=Σₙ≥0 aₙxⁿ. Treat it as a formal power series; no convergence assumption is required for this algebraic derivation.
Multiply the recurrence by xⁿ and sum for n≥1: A(x)−a₀=3xA(x)+2x/(1−x). Substitute a₀=1.
Partial fractions give A(x)=−1/(1−x)+2/(1−3x). Check the numerator: −(1−3x)+2(1−x)=1+x.
Use 1/(1−cx)=Σcⁿxⁿ. Comparing coefficients gives aₙ=−1+2·3ⁿ.
The first four values from the formula are 1,5,17,53. Direct recurrence gives 3×1+2=5, then 17, then 53, agreeing with the formula.
For an independent check, aₙ+1=3(aₙ₋₁+1), so the shifted sequence is geometric with starting value 2.
long.trap: The sum starts at n=1, so the left side is A(x)−a₀, not A(x).

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
long.title: A cyclic group homomorphism and its kernel
long.prompt: Let φ:Z₁₂→Z₄ be φ([x]₁₂)=[x]₄, with both groups using addition. Show it is well-defined and a homomorphism; find its kernel, image, and the order of [8]₁₂.
steps: Well-definedness matters because group elements are residue classes. If x≡y mod 12, then x−y is divisible by 12 and hence by 4, so [x]₄=[y]₄.
For any residue classes, φ([x]₁₂+[y]₁₂)=[x+y]₄=[x]₄+[y]₄. Therefore φ preserves the operation and is a group homomorphism.
The kernel consists of x with x≡0 mod 4. Within Z₁₂ it is {0,4,8}. It is a subgroup, and it is normal because Z₁₂ is Abelian.
Every class 0,1,2,3 in Z₄ is attained, so the image is all Z₄ and φ is surjective. It is not injective since the kernel has three elements.
The four cosets are {0,4,8}, {1,5,9}, {2,6,10}, {3,7,11}. Adding cosets follows addition modulo 4, giving Z₁₂/kerφ ≅ Z₄.
The order of [8]₁₂ is the least positive k with 8k≡0 mod 12. The multiples are 8,4,0, so its order is 3; equivalently 12/gcd(12,8)=3.
The counting check |Z₁₂|=|kerφ|·|imφ| gives 12=3×4. Do not call φ an isomorphism: surjectivity alone is insufficient.
long.answer: kerφ={0,4,8}; imφ=Z₄; order([8]₁₂)=3; φ is surjective but not injective.
long.trap: For the additive group, powers mean repeated addition; use 8k mod 12, not 8ᵏ mod 12.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:alg
long.title: Shortest paths and Euler/Hamilton properties
long.prompt: Consider the undirected weighted graph with vertices A,B,C,D,E and edges AB=2, AC=5, BC=1, BD=4, CD=1, CE=6, DE=2. Find shortest paths from A, then test whether the graph has an Euler trail and a Hamilton path.
steps: All weights are positive, so Dijkstra’s algorithm applies. Initialise d(A)=0 and all other distances to infinity. After settling A, d(B)=2 and d(C)=5.
Settle B at distance 2. Relax BC to set d(C)=3 via B; relax BD to set d(D)=6 via B.
Settle C at 3. Edge CD improves d(D) to 4 via C; CE sets d(E)=9.
Settle D at 4. Edge DE improves d(E) to 6. Settling E finishes: distances A=0,B=2,C=3,D=4,E=6.
The shortest A-to-E route follows predecessors A→B→C→D→E with total 2+1+1+2=6. The direct route through AC and CE is longer at 11.
Degrees are deg(A)=2,deg(B)=3,deg(C)=4,deg(D)=3,deg(E)=2. Exactly B and D have odd degree, so the connected graph has an Euler trail from B to D but no Euler circuit. One trail is B–A–C–B–D–C–E–D.
A Hamilton path visits vertices exactly once; A–B–C–D–E is one. Unlike the Euler trail, it need not use every edge. Weights affect shortest paths but not these existence checks.
long.answer: Shortest distances 0,2,3,4,6; Euler trail B–A–C–B–D–C–E–D; Hamilton path A–B–C–D–E.
long.trap: Euler uses every edge once; Hamilton uses every vertex once. They are different requirements.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
long.title: Binary search with interval invariants
long.prompt: Use iterative binary search to find 23 in [3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31,35]. Show low,high,mid for each iteration using zero-based inclusive bounds, and then trace a failed search for 20.
steps: Set low=0 and high=8. Maintain that any matching index must lie within the inclusive interval [low,high]. Calculate mid=low+(high−low)//2.
For key 23: (low,high,mid)=(0,8,4), value 19. Since 23>19, set low=5.
The next interval gives (5,8,6), value 27; set high=5. Then (5,5,5), value 23, so return index 5 after three midpoint comparisons.
For key 20: start (0,8,4) at 19 and set low=5; then (5,8,6) at 27 and set high=5; then (5,5,5) at 23 and set high=4.
Now low=5>high=4, so the interval is empty and return −1. Do not examine an array element after the interval has become empty.
Pseudocode: while low<=high: mid=low+(high-low)//2; if a[mid]==key:return mid; if a[mid]<key:low=mid+1; else:high=mid-1. After the loop return −1.
Each unsuccessful iteration discards at least about half the remaining interval, giving O(log n) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary space. The array must be sorted in the comparison order.
long.answer: 23 is at index 5; 20 is absent and returns −1.
long.trap: With inclusive high, use high=mid−1 and low=mid+1. Failing to exclude mid can cause an infinite loop.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
long.title: Trace a circular queue with explicit count
long.prompt: A circular queue of capacity 5 uses front for the next removal, rear for the next insertion, and a count. Start at front=rear=count=0. Enqueue 10,20,30; dequeue twice; enqueue 40,50,60,70; dequeue once. Trace its states.
steps: Use enqueue only when count<5: store at rear, set rear=(rear+1)%5, increment count. Dequeue only when count>0: read front, advance it modulo 5, decrement count.
After enqueueing 10,20,30, front=0,rear=3,count=3 and logical order is [10,20,30].
The two dequeues return 10 and 20. Now front=2,rear=3,count=1, with [30]. Old array contents at removed positions are not live queue elements.
Enqueue 40 at index 3 and 50 at index 4. Rear wraps to 0; front=2,rear=0,count=3, logical order [30,40,50].
Enqueue 60 at index 0 and 70 at index 1. Now front=2,rear=2,count=5, logical order [30,40,50,60,70]. The queue is full although front equals rear.

The final dequeue returns 30 and leaves front=3,rear=2,count=4. Logical order is [40,50,60,70]. All positions of the five-slot array can be used because the explicit count distinguishes full from empty.
Each operation takes O(1) time. A different representation reserving one empty slot would use a different full condition; do not mix that convention with the count-based one.
long.answer: Removed values: 10,20,30. Final queue [40,50,60,70], front=3,rear=2,count=4.
long.trap: Here rear denotes the next insertion position, not the last occupied position.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
long.title: Delete all matching nodes from a singly linked list
long.prompt: Write a C++ function erase_all(Node*& head,int key) that deletes every node with the key. Trace it on 7→7→2→7→3→NULL with key=7 and explain why consecutive matches are not skipped.
steps: Assume struct Node {int value; Node* next;}; and nodes were allocated individually with new. The function must be allowed to update the caller’s head, so take Node*&.
Use a pointer to the link that currently owns a node: Node** link=&head;. Initially it addresses the head pointer; later it may address a previous node’s next field.
Function: void erase_all(Node*& head,int key){Node** link=&head;while(*link){if((*link)->value==key){Node* victim=*link;*link=victim->next;delete victim;}else{link=&((*link)->next);}}}.
For the first 7, replace head with its successor and delete that node. Keep link pointing at head so the next 7 is checked; removing it leaves 2→7→3.
Value 2 does not match, so move link to the address of that node’s next field. The next 7 matches: splice it out and delete it, leaving 2→3.
Check 3, advance to its null next link, and stop. The final list is 2→3→NULL, with all three 7 nodes freed exactly once.
The loop visits each node once: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. It also handles an empty list and a list containing only matches. The caller must eventually free remaining nodes.
long.answer: Final list: 2→3→NULL; three nodes deleted; O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
long.trap: Do not advance the owning link after deleting a match; the successor may contain the same key.

Value 2 does not match, so move link to the address of that node’s next field. The next 7 matches: splice it out and delete it, leaving 2→3.
Check 3, advance to its null next link, and stop. The final list is 2→3→NULL, with all three 7 nodes freed exactly once.
The loop visits each node once: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. It also handles an empty list and a list containing only matches. The caller must eventually free remaining nodes.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
long.title: BST insertion and two-child deletion
long.prompt: Insert 50,30,70,20,40,60,80 into an empty BST, then delete 50 using its inorder successor. Give the final links and all three depth-first traversals.
steps: Insert 50 as root; 30 goes left and 70 right. Then 20 and 40 become the left and right children of 30; 60 and 80 become the left and right children of 70.
The root 50 has two children. Its inorder successor is the minimum key in its right subtree: follow 70’s left link to find 60.
Replace the root key 50 with 60, then delete the original node containing 60 from the right subtree. That original node is a leaf, so set 70’s left link to NULL.
The final root is 60. Its left child 30 has children 20 and 40; its right child 70 has only right child 80. There are six nodes after deleting exactly one key.
The inorder list is sorted and contains every original key except 50, confirming both the BST order and deletion result.

Finding and removing a successor costs O(h), where h is the tree height. A plain BST can have h=Θ(n) for an unfortunate insertion order; this operation is not guaranteed logarithmic without a balancing rule.
long.answer: Final root 60; inorder 20,30,40,60,70,80.
long.trap: After copying the successor key, also remove its original node; otherwise 60 appears twice.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:dsa
long.title: Build and use a max heap
long.prompt: Use bottom-up heap construction on [4,10,3,5,1], then perform heap sort. Show the heap after building and the active heap after every extraction.
steps: Use zero-based children 2i+1 and 2i+2. Start sifting down at floor(n/2)−1=1. Node 10 already exceeds children 5 and 1.
Sift down root 4: swap with larger child 10, giving [10,4,3,5,1]; then swap 4 with child 5, giving the max heap [10,5,3,4,1].
Swap root with the last active entry: [1,5,3,4,10]. Restore the size-4 heap by swaps 1↔5 then 1↔4, giving [5,4,3,1 | 10].
Swap 5 with the last active entry and restore size 3: [1,4,3 | 5,10] becomes [4,1,3 | 5,10].
Extract 4: swapping with 3 leaves [3,1 | 4,5,10], already a size-2 heap. Extract 3 to obtain [1 | 3,4,5,10].
The final ascending array is [1,3,4,5,10]. The bar separates the active heap from the sorted suffix; the suffix is never included in later heap restoration.
Bottom-up construction takes O(n); the n−1 extractions each cost at most O(log n), giving O(n log n) total time. Standard in-place heap sort uses O(1) auxiliary storage and is not stable.
long.answer: Built heap [10,5,3,4,1]; final sorted array [1,3,4,5,10].
long.trap: Reduce the active heap size before sifting down; otherwise a sorted maximum can re-enter the heap.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
long.title: Evaluate a career choice through self-exploration
long.prompt: A student chooses a career only because friends call it prestigious, but dislikes its daily work. Explain how self-exploration can produce a better decision without dismissing income or family responsibilities.
steps: Define self-exploration as examining a proposal within oneself and validating it in living, rather than accepting it merely because of social pressure or authority.
Identify the assumption: “prestige alone will ensure lasting happiness.” Separate this from the student’s real aspirations for meaningful work, relationships and adequate physical facilities.

Use natural acceptance as a criterion to explore whether responsible work and mutually respectful relationships are desirable. Distinguish it from a temporary attraction to a title or a dislike produced by one difficult class.

Assess the actual options: daily tasks, learning effort, strengths, improvement needs, income sufficient for responsibilities and likely effects on relationships. These practical facts are part of the decision, not distractions from values.

Experimentally validate the proposal through a small project, internship observation, conversations with practitioners and an honest study trial. Record whether the work supports both competence and a responsible way of living.
Discuss the findings respectfully with family. Choose a provisional path supported by understanding and evidence; set review points rather than making prestige an unquestionable rule.
Conclude with the priority of right understanding, relationship and physical facility. Income matters as a facility, while prestige alone cannot guarantee continuous happiness.

long.trap: Self-exploration is neither blind obedience to others nor an excuse to follow every short-lived preference.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
long.title: A balanced exam routine using sanyam and health
long.prompt: A student studies late every night, skips meals and feels that buying another device will solve low concentration. Analyse the situation using the distinction between self and body, sanyam and health.
steps: Identify the two dimensions: anxiety, comparison and unclear priorities concern the self; insufficient rest and irregular food concern the body. One purchase does not automatically resolve either dimension.
Explain sanyam as the feeling of responsibility in the self for nurturing, protecting and rightly using the body. It involves deliberate choices rather than treating the body as an unlimited machine.
Explain health as harmony in the body and its ability to function as an instrument of the self. In this study case, regular routines support that aim; the answer need not give medical diagnoses.

Propose an achievable study plan with bounded focused sessions, regular meals, sufficient rest and movement breaks. Prioritise unfinished and weak syllabus topics rather than extending unproductive hours indefinitely.

Assess physical facilities realistically: a working device and required books may already be sufficient. Buy only when a concrete learning need is unmet, rather than using comparison as the criterion.

For the self, use clear goals, self-evaluation and respectful support from classmates. Review whether the plan improves actual understanding and the ability to write answers, not merely time spent near a screen.

Conclude that prosperity is based on an accurate assessment of physical need, while sanyam connects responsible intention to daily care of the body. Sustained preparation requires both understanding and bodily support.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
long.title: Restore trust and justice in a project team
long.prompt: A teammate misses a deadline. Others mock their ability and exclude them without discussion. Analyse the conflict using trust, respect, intention/competence and justice, then propose a fair response.
steps: Describe trust in the UHV sense as assurance about the other person’s intention for mutual happiness. A missed deadline is evidence of an outcome; it does not by itself establish an intention to harm the group.
Distinguish intention from competence by hearing the teammate’s account and examining task clarity, skill gaps, workload and communication. Do not assume every explanation removes responsibility.
Respect means right evaluation of a human being, not ranking their human worth by one performance. Public mockery confuses a limited skill or mistake with the person’s value.

Apply justice through recognition of relationship and its values, fulfilment of responsibilities, evaluation of outcomes and mutual happiness. Identify both the team’s legitimate need for delivery and the teammate’s right to respectful treatment.

Agree a repair plan: divide the unfinished work clearly, assign a competent support partner if needed, set a realistic checkpoint and state how progress will be reported. The teammate acknowledges the impact and contributes to the repair.

Use care and guidance to build competence, gratitude for useful contributions and affection for a sense of relatedness. Consequences should address task reliability fairly instead of humiliating the person.
Conclude with a future team agreement: clear roles, early reporting of blockers and evidence-based review. This supports fearlessness and cooperation while preserving accountability.
long.answer: A fair response combines respectful evaluation, clear responsibility, practical repair and competence-building.
long.trap: Justice is more than punishment, and trust does not require ignoring repeated failures or unverified claims.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
long.title: Design a campus resource cycle
long.prompt: A campus wastes water, mixes all refuse and repeatedly replaces repairable devices. Use the four orders and mutual fulfilment to design a responsible improvement plan.
steps: Map the four orders: water, soil, metals and buildings are material; campus trees and vegetation are plant/bio; birds and other animals are animal; students, staff and decision-makers are human.
Explain that the orders are interconnected. Water quality affects plants and animals, while human extraction and disposal can either support or disturb existing relationships.

For water, measure use, repair leaks, reduce avoidable consumption and use appropriately treated water where suitable. Set a baseline and inspect actual reduction rather than assuming a campaign alone solved the issue.

For waste, separate streams at source, reduce unnecessary material use and route each stream to suitable processing. Organic material can support biological cycles when correctly managed; plastics and electronic waste do not become harmless merely by being called recyclable.

For devices, assess the real requirement, maintain and repair usable equipment, share underused facilities and send end-of-life electronics to an appropriate recovery route. This reduces extraction and unmanaged disposal.

Assign human responsibilities: explain the reasons, provide understandable collection points, train the people involved and review records of water use, repairs and material recovery. Technical design and responsible behavior must work together.

Conclude with mutual fulfilment: facilities should meet human needs while supporting conditions for other orders. Avoid claiming a perfectly closed cycle; some losses and impacts remain and should be measured and reduced.
long.answer: Reduce demand, maintain resources, separate waste, repair devices and verify results across all four orders.
long.trap: Nature’s cycles do not justify unlimited consumption or the claim that every synthetic material safely returns to nature.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:uhv
long.title: An ethical software-release decision
long.prompt: A student team discovers that its attendance app sometimes marks the wrong person present. A sponsor wants an immediate launch and asks the team to hide the defect. Apply professional ethics and propose a reasoned response.
steps: State the conflict clearly: pressure for a successful-looking launch conflicts with truthful reporting, reliability and the interests of students and staff affected by incorrect records.

Use right understanding and natural acceptance to evaluate the proposal. Knowingly concealing a demonstrated defect undermines trust; a technically impressive interface does not remove the responsibility for accurate behavior.

Establish the evidence: reproduce the defect with appropriate test data, record affected scenarios and estimate its scope. Distinguish verified findings from assumptions, and avoid exposing unnecessary personal records during testing.
Inform the responsible stakeholders accurately. Explain the user impact, available evidence, proposed repair and the limits of present confidence. Do not claim the issue is fixed before retesting.

Choose a proportionate release plan: delay the affected function or use a clearly disclosed limited pilot with a verified manual check until the defect is corrected. Protect already recorded data and provide a way to correct errors.
Improve competence through root-cause analysis, focused tests, review and monitoring. Assign ownership for the fix and review outcomes with the people affected.

Conclude that ethical professional conduct integrates truthfulness, responsibility and competent action. A sustainable relationship with the sponsor is based on verified value and trust, not concealed failure.
long.answer: Disclose the verified defect, protect affected records, repair and retest, then release with honest limitations.
long.trap: Do not frame honesty and technical quality as competing goals; trustworthy engineering requires both.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
long.title: Debug indentation and loop placement
long.prompt: A program should sum [2,4,6] and print 12 once. Explain and correct these two faults: a loop body without indentation, and print(total) indented inside the loop.
steps: Python uses indentation to delimit a loop body. The source "for x in [2,4,6]:\ntotal += x" has no indented suite, so it raises IndentationError before the loop can execute.
Initialise total=0 before the loop. Otherwise, even correctly indented total += x tries to read an undefined name and raises NameError.
With total=0, if both total += x and print(total) are inside the loop, the program prints the running sums 2,6,12 on separate lines.
To print only the final sum, keep the update inside the loop and dedent the print to the same level as for.

Correct program:
total = 0
for x in [2, 4, 6]:
    total += x
print(total)
Trace total before and after each update: 0→2→6→12. The print runs only after all three iterations, producing one line: 12.
Test an empty list: with the same initial value and print placement, the program prints 0. This confirms the accumulator is initialised outside the loop.
long.answer: Correct output is a single line: 12.
long.trap: A program can be syntactically valid but still logically wrong because a statement is in the wrong indentation block.

long.title: Dictionary counts and birthday lookup

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
long.title: A loss-aware combine_lists function
long.prompt: Write combine_lists(keys,values) that rejects unequal lengths and duplicate keys. Demonstrate it on ["DE","OOP","PY"] and [70,80,90], and explain two failure cases.
steps: Define the input contract: keys and values are sized sequences; keys must be hashable, lengths must match, and duplicate keys are rejected instead of silently overwriting.
For keys ["DE","OOP","PY"] and values [70,80,90], the returned mapping is {"DE":70,"OOP":80,"PY":90}. Every supplied pair is represented once.
For ["A","B"] and [1], the length check raises ValueError("Different lengths") before any pairing can silently discard a key.
For ["A","A"] and [1,2], the second occurrence raises ValueError("Duplicate key"). Without this guard, a dictionary comprehension would keep only A:2.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
long.title: Collision detection without square roots
long.prompt: Implement ball_collide for finite real (x,y,r) tuples with nonnegative radii. Test balls A=(−1,2,2), B=(2,6,3) and C=(3,6,3), treating touching as collision.
steps: Let dx and dy be centre-coordinate differences. Two disks overlap or touch when centre distance ≤ r1+r2. Since both sides are nonnegative, compare their squares to avoid computing a square root.

Function:
def ball_collide(a,b):
    x1,y1,r1 = a
    x2,y2,r2 = b
    if r1 < 0 or r2 < 0:
        raise ValueError("Radii must be nonnegative")
    return (x1-x2)**2 + (y1-y2)**2 <= (r1+r2)**2
For A and B, dx²+dy²=(−1−2)²+(2−6)²=9+16=25. The squared radius sum is (2+3)²=25, so they touch and return True.
For A and C, the squared distance is (−1−3)²+(2−6)²=16+16=32. Since 32>25, return False.
For identical zero-radius balls at the same point, both sides are 0 and the stated touching convention returns True. A negative radius is rejected.
The function performs a constant number of arithmetic operations, so it is O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space under the usual arithmetic model.

Floating-point measurements near the boundary may need an application-specific tolerance, but do not silently alter the exercise’s exact <= rule. Also validate finiteness if accepting untrusted numeric inputs.
long.answer: ball_collide(A,B)=True; ball_collide(A,C)=False.
long.trap: Use <=, not <, when touching counts as collision.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
long.title: Exactly one edit between two strings
long.prompt: Implement nearly_equal for exactly one insertion, deletion or substitution. Test ("book","books"), ("book","boon"), ("book","book"), ("book","back") and ("","a").
steps: Define the contract before coding: exactly one character edit is permitted; zero edits is False, and swapping two adjacent characters is not a separate allowed operation.
Arrange the inputs so a is no longer than b. A length difference greater than 1 immediately rules out a single edit.

Function:
def nearly_equal(a,b):
    if len(a)>len(b): a,b=b,a
    if len(b)-len(a)>1: return False
    i=j=edits=0
    while i<len(a) and j<len(b):
        if a[i]==b[j]:
            i+=1; j+=1
        else:
            edits+=1
            if edits>1: return False
            if len(a)==len(b): i+=1
            j+=1
    edits += (len(a)-i)+(len(b)-j)
    return edits==1
When lengths are equal, a mismatch consumes one character from each string, representing substitution. When lengths differ, consume only from the longer string, representing insertion/deletion.
Test results in the requested order are True,True,False,False,True. book→books adds s; book→boon replaces k; equal strings need no edit; book→back changes two positions.
The remaining suffix contributes any last unmatched character. This makes the empty-string case ("","a") work while ("","") remains False.
The scan is O(n+m) time and O(1) extra space. Python string elements here are Unicode code points; visually combined characters may consist of multiple code points.
long.answer: True, True, False, False, True.
long.trap: Returning edits<=1 would incorrectly accept identical strings under the exactly-one-edit contract.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
long.title: Prefix products, reversal and one-line arithmetic helpers
long.prompt: Implement cumulative_product and a nonmutating reverse without list.reverse(). Define one-line gcd and lcm helpers. Trace [3,−2,0,5] and the pair (−18,24).
steps:
Prefix-product code:
def cumulative_product(a):
    result, product = [],1
    for x in a:
        product *= x
        result.append(product)
    return result
For [3,−2,0,5], the running products are 3,−6,0,0. A zero makes every later prefix product zero, even when later values are nonzero.
Nonmutating reversal can be one line: def reverse(a): return a[::-1]. The result is [5,0,−2,3], while the input retains its original order. An empty list gives [].
One-line Euclidean helper: gcd = lambda a,b: abs(a) if b==0 else gcd(b,a%b). One-line LCM helper: lcm = lambda a,b: 0 if a==0 or b==0 else abs(a//gcd(a,b)*b).
For (−18,24), gcd is 6 and lcm is 72. Using // before multiplication keeps integer arithmetic; the absolute value produces the nonnegative convention.
Test gcd(0,0)=0 under this implementation, lcm(0,0)=0, cumulative_product([])=[] and reverse([])=[]. The LCM zero branch prevents division by zero.

Both list functions take O(n) time and O(n) result space. The recursive gcd uses O(log min(|a|,|b|)) steps for positive nonzero magnitudes and also uses recursion-stack space; very large inputs can reach Python’s recursion limit.
long.answer: Products [3,−6,0,0]; reverse [5,0,−2,3]; gcd=6; lcm=72.
long.trap: The multiplicative accumulator starts at 1. Starting at 0 would make every product zero.

long.subject: cia-2-2025-26:py
long.title: Analyse missing marks and produce a labelled chart
long.prompt: Using pandas, NumPy and Matplotlib, analyse marks [60,80,missing,100] for four students. Report the missing count and mean without silently treating the missing mark as zero, then plot available values.
steps: Set up a local environment and install dependencies with python -m pip install numpy pandas matplotlib. Keep package installation separate from the analysis script.
Create the data: import numpy as np; import pandas as pd; import matplotlib.pyplot as plt; df=pd.DataFrame({"student":["A","B","C","D"],"marks":[60,80,np.nan,100]}).
Inspect the missing count with int(df["marks"].isna().sum()), which gives 1. A missing observation is not automatically a score of zero.
Compute df["marks"].mean(); pandas excludes the missing entry by default here, so the mean of available marks is (60+80+100)/3=80. State that only three observed marks contribute.

Create observed=df.dropna(subset=["marks"]). Plot plt.bar(observed["student"],observed["marks"]); plt.xlabel("Student"); plt.ylabel("Marks"); plt.title("Available marks; one score missing"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show().
The bars are A=60,B=80,D=100. Student C has no plotted score; the title/description explains the missing value instead of implying C scored zero.

If this data came from an HTTP request, requests should use a timeout and verify the response before parsing. A Flask route can expose a summary in a separate web application, but neither package is necessary for this local chart.
long.answer: 1 missing mark; observed mean 80; plotted values 60,80,100.
long.trap: Filling the missing mark with zero changes the mean to 60 and asserts information not present in the data.
